llm/debugging-llm-applications.i: I capture full traces, separate retrieval, prompt, model and parsing problems, fix one change at a time, and add regression tests.

prompting/anatomy-of-a-good-prompt.s: Write the prompt as a brief for a capable new colleague who has never seen your project: purpose, material, limits, and the shape of the answer you expect.
prompting/anatomy-of-a-good-prompt.i: I write prompts with task, context, material, constraints and format, separate data from instructions, and test on varied inputs.

prompting/examples-and-few-shot-promptin.s: Examples are worked answers in the margin. A student will copy their shape, so pick ones you would be happy to see repeated.
prompting/examples-and-few-shot-promptin.i: I use few-shot examples well: varied, consistent, realistic and separate from my test set.

prompting/reasoning-and-step-by-step-pro.s: Reasoning prompts give the model scrap paper. Useful for hard sums, wasteful for simple ones, and the scrap paper should never be handed to the customer.
prompting/reasoning-and-step-by-step-pro.i: I use step-by-step prompting where it pays off, separate reasoning from the final answer, and verify rather than trust explanations.

prompting/system-prompts-roles-and-conte.s: The system prompt is the house rules pinned to the wall, in view of every visitor. Do not pin the safe combination next to them.
prompting/system-prompts-roles-and-conte.i: I structure prompts with system messages and tags, place long documents well, and treat untrusted text as data, not instructions.

prompting/structured-output-json-and-sch.s: A schema is a form with tick boxes. The fewer free-text boxes you leave, the fewer surprises when the forms arrive at the next desk.
prompting/structured-output-json-and-sch.i: I define schemas, choose a structured output method, parse strictly, and design shapes that are easy for models to fill in.

prompting/validating-repairing-and-retry.s: Treat model output like input from a stranger: check the envelope, check the contents, and keep a procedure for letters that do not make sense.
prompting/validating-repairing-and-retry.i: I validate in layers, retry with feedback within limits, repair only safe things, and design fallbacks and review paths.

prompting/prompt-versioning-and-testing.s: A prompt with no version history is a script edited live on the server. It works until it does not, and then nobody knows what changed.
prompting/prompt-versioning-and-testing.i: I version prompts as files, review them, run evaluations in CI, and roll out and back with traceable versions.

prompting/debugging-bad-prompts.s: Debugging a prompt is like debugging a flaky test: capture the failure, shrink it, change one variable, and keep the test.
prompting/debugging-bad-prompts.i: I reproduce failures, isolate causes, apply targeted fixes, measure on the whole set, and keep regression tests.

claude-skills/what-a-claude-skill-is.s: A skill is a binder on the shelf with a clear label on the spine. Claude reads the labels all the time, and takes down a binder only when the job calls for it.
claude-skills/what-a-claude-skill-is.i: I explain what a skill is, how it differs from prompts and tools, and choose when a skill is worth writing.

claude-skills/anatomy-of-a-skill-folder.s: Treat the folder like a small project README plus tools: one clear entry point, linked chapters, and nothing a reviewer cannot find in minutes.
claude-skills/anatomy-of-a-skill-folder.i: I lay out a skill with a proper header, a focused body, and supporting files, and keep it reviewable.

claude-skills/writing-descriptions-that-.s: The description is the spine label on the binder. If it says "Stuff", nobody takes it down. If it says "Everything", people take down the wrong binder.
claude-skills/writing-descriptions-that-.i: I write descriptions that say what and when, balance breadth, and test triggering with near-miss requests.

claude-skills/progressive-disclosure-and.s: Like a good manual: a one-page quick start, then chapters you open only when you need them, not a thousand pages pushed across the desk.
claude-skills/progressive-disclosure-and.i: I structure skills in layers, move rare detail to linked files, keep links shallow, and measure size against value.

claude-skills/scripts-and-deterministic-.s: The model is the editor and the script is the calculator. Do not ask the editor to add up the column by eye.
claude-skills/scripts-and-deterministic-.i: I put exact work in tested scripts with clear output, keep them safe, and let the model handle judgement.

claude-skills/testing-and-evaluating-a-s.s: Testing a skill is a driving test with and without the instructor. If the learner passes without, the instructor was not needed.
claude-skills/testing-and-evaluating-a-s.i: I test triggering, quality and cost, compare with a baseline, iterate one change at a time, and keep records.

claude-skills/sharing-versioning-and-ski.s: Installing a skill is hiring a helper who will follow written instructions with your keys in the room. Check the references first.
claude-skills/sharing-versioning-and-ski.i: I share skills through version control, version and own them, and review skills for security before use.

claude-skills/debugging-skills-that-do-n.s: Walk the path the way Claude does: can it find the binder, does the label make it pick it up, does it follow the pages, and do the tools in the binder work?
claude-skills/debugging-skills-that-do-n.i: I debug skills in order: discovery, choosing, following and scripts, and lock fixes in with tests.

mcp/why-tools-and-what-mcp-is.s: MCP is a universal plug for AI tools. It makes connecting easy; it does not check what is behind the socket.
mcp/why-tools-and-what-mcp-is.i: I explain why models need tools, what MCP standardises, its three roles, and what it does not guarantee.

mcp/function-calling-and-tool-schemas.s: A tool definition is the manual you tape to a machine for a user who reads very fast and never asks questions. Be precise.
mcp/function-calling-and-tool-schemas.i: I write clear tool definitions with schemas, validate arguments in code, and keep the toolset small and focused.

mcp/the-tool-use-loop.s: Think of a relay race: the model hands the baton to your code, your code runs and hands it back with the result. Put a timer on the race.
mcp/the-tool-use-loop.i: I implement the tool-use loop with correct results, error handling, limits and logging.

mcp/mcp-architecture-hosts-clients-serve.s: MCP is a polite conversation: introduce yourselves and say what you can do, then ask and answer in a fixed format. Keep side chatter off the main line.
mcp/mcp-architecture-hosts-clients-serve.i: I explain the MCP lifecycle, messages and transports, and avoid common protocol mistakes such as polluting stdout.

mcp/building-an-mcp-server-in-python.s: Building a server is writing a tiny API for a reader who only sees your docstrings. Test it with a human-friendly tool before connecting any model.
mcp/building-an-mcp-server-in-python.i: I build a small MCP server in Python, test it with the inspector, and register it with a host.

mcp/resources-prompts-and-other-primitiv.s: Tools are the machines in the workshop, resources are the reference books you can put on the bench, and prompts are the recipe cards you choose to start from.
mcp/resources-prompts-and-other-primitiv.i: I choose between tools, resources and prompts, and use each primitive for what it is good at.

mcp/permissions-auth-and-prompt-injectio.s: Assume the assistant can be talked into things. Give it a small toolbox, a supervisor for risky jobs, and keep the vault, the stranger's letters and the front door out of the same room.
mcp/permissions-auth-and-prompt-injectio.i: I apply least privilege, require approval for risky actions, authenticate remote servers properly, and design against prompt injection.

mcp/debugging-tool-use-and-mcp.s: Debug from the bottom of the stack up: the tool, the wire, the menu, the diner who orders, and the waiter who carries the plates.
mcp/debugging-tool-use-and-mcp.i: I debug tool use layer by layer, use the inspector and traces, and add tests for tool lists, definitions and loops.

cloud-iam/identities-principals-and-perm.s: A cloud request is a door with a guard: the guard checks your badge, your name on the list, and the rule for that room.
cloud-iam/identities-principals-and-perm.i: I separate authentication from authorization, name the parts of a decision, and prefer workload identities to stored keys.

cloud-iam/aws-iam-policies-roles-and-ass.s: A role is a hotel key card that works for a few hours and only opens the rooms listed on it.
cloud-iam/aws-iam-policies-roles-and-ass.i: I read IAM policies, use roles for workloads and cross-account access, and use boundaries as guardrails.

cloud-iam/azure-entra-id-rbac-and-manage.s: Entra ID is the passport office; Azure RBAC is the list of doors each passport opens.
cloud-iam/azure-entra-id-rbac-and-manage.i: I assign roles at the right scope, prefer managed identities, and protect privileged access.

cloud-iam/least-privilege-and-access-rev.s: Least privilege is a gardener pruning: access grows back unless you cut it on a schedule.
cloud-iam/least-privilege-and-access-rev.i: I narrow permissions with usage data, design roles for jobs, and review access regularly.

cloud-iam/secrets-and-encryption-with-km.s: A secrets manager is a bank vault with a logbook: you ask at the counter, every opening is written down.
cloud-iam/secrets-and-encryption-with-km.i: I keep secrets in a managed store, use KMS and envelope encryption, and rotate with overlap.

cloud-iam/network-boundaries-and-private.s: The network is the fence and identity is the lock. A fence without a lock, or a lock on an open field, is only half a plan.
cloud-iam/network-boundaries-and-private.i: I keep resources private, narrow security rules, use private endpoints and block public storage access.

cloud-iam/logging-detection-and-audit-tr.s: Audit logs are the security camera footage of your cloud. Footage that is switched off or stored in the thief's pocket helps nobody.
cloud-iam/logging-detection-and-audit-tr.i: I enable audit logging everywhere, protect it, and alert on high-risk actions.

cloud-iam/debugging-access-denied-and-cl.s: Debug access like a locksmith: find which lock refused, which key you used, and why, before you cut any new doors.
cloud-iam/debugging-access-denied-and-cl.i: I debug access-denied errors in order, fix them narrowly, and respond to leaked credentials by containing first.

k8s-ops/the-control-plane-in-depth.s: The API server is the front desk, etcd is the filing cabinet, controllers are the clerks who keep the files true.
k8s-ops/the-control-plane-in-depth.i: I can trace a request through the control plane and predict what each failure means.

k8s-ops/etcd-backup-and-restore.s: An etcd backup is a spare key. It only counts once you have tried it in the lock.
k8s-ops/etcd-backup-and-restore.i: I take verified etcd snapshots, store them safely and rehearse restores.

k8s-ops/upgrading-clusters-safely.s: An upgrade is a staircase: one step at a time, handrail first, and you check the next step before you put weight on it.
k8s-ops/upgrading-clusters-safely.i: I plan upgrades one minor version at a time, scan for deprecated APIs and keep a rollback.

k8s-ops/rbac-and-service-accounts.s: RBAC is a set of sticky notes: each says who may do which verb on which thing. There is no note that says no.
k8s-ops/rbac-and-service-accounts.i: I write narrow Roles and bindings, give workloads their own service accounts and audit with can-i.

k8s-ops/nodes-draining-taints-and-capaci.s: Draining a node is evicting tenants politely: tell them where to go, check the building rules (budgets), then lock the door.
k8s-ops/nodes-draining-taints-and-capaci.i: I drain nodes safely, use PDBs, taints and spread rules, and keep spare capacity.

k8s-ops/resource-quotas-limits-and-autos.s: Requests are your table reservation, limits are the rule about how much you can eat, and quotas are how many tables your team may book.
k8s-ops/resource-quotas-limits-and-autos.i: I set requests and limits, apply quotas and defaults, and use autoscaling with correct inputs.

k8s-ops/network-policies-and-pod-securit.s: A flat cluster network is an open-plan office: anyone can wander into the finance room. Policies add doors and badges.
k8s-ops/network-policies-and-pod-securit.i: I apply default-deny network policies, Pod Security Standards and hardened security contexts.

k8s-ops/debugging-cluster-and-node-probl.s: Debugging a cluster is peeling an onion from the outside: pod, then node, then control plane, and checking each layer before moving in.
k8s-ops/debugging-cluster-and-node-probl.i: I triage cluster faults in order, read node conditions, and check the control plane and certificates.

argocd/pull-based-delivery-and-the-repos.s: Push delivery is a courier who comes to your door. Pull delivery is a thermostat that keeps checking the target and adjusts.
argocd/pull-based-delivery-and-the-repos.i: I explain pull-based delivery, drift and why the repository is the source of truth.

argocd/installing-argo-cd-and-the-applic.s: The Application resource is a delivery order: pick up from this address (repository), drop at that address (namespace).
argocd/installing-argo-cd-and-the-applic.i: I install Argo CD, understand its components, and write an Application.

argocd/sync-health-and-drift.s: Sync status asks "is it what we wrote?" Health asks "does it work?" You need both answers before you act.
argocd/sync-health-and-drift.i: I read sync and health separately, use prune and self-heal carefully, and ignore expected differences.

argocd/helm-and-kustomize-with-argo-cd.s: Argo CD uses Helm like a printing press: it prints the pages and puts them on the wall, it does not keep Helm's own notebook.
argocd/helm-and-kustomize-with-argo-cd.i: I deliver Helm and Kustomize sources, keep values in the repository and pin versions.

argocd/environments-app-of-apps-and-appl.s: App-of-apps is a table of contents. An ApplicationSet is a stamp: one design, many copies.
argocd/environments-app-of-apps-and-appl.i: I organise environments with overlays, app-of-apps and ApplicationSets and promote by commit.

argocd/hooks-sync-waves-and-progressive-.s: Waves are the order of courses at dinner, hooks are the chef tasting before and after, and a canary is the first small plate sent to one table.
argocd/hooks-sync-waves-and-progressive-.i: I order syncs with waves and hooks and understand canary and blue-green rollouts.

argocd/access-projects-secrets-and-multi.s: Argo CD holds the keys to many clusters. Treat it as production infrastructure, not a developer toy.
argocd/access-projects-secrets-and-multi.i: I scope teams with projects and RBAC, keep secrets out of the repository and secure multi-cluster setups.

argocd/debugging-argo-cd.s: Walk the pipeline in order: can it fetch, can it render, can it apply, is it healthy? The first "no" is your problem.
argocd/debugging-argo-cd.i: I debug Argo CD by stage, reproduce renders locally and fix OutOfSync loops.

system-design/the-design-method-and-esti.s: Designing is like planning a bridge: you ask how many cars, then how strong, then what if a pier fails, before you pour any concrete.
system-design/the-design-method-and-esti.i: I follow a fixed design method and size a system with round-number estimates.

system-design/caching-without-stampedes.s: A cache is a shelf of photocopies; when the shelf empties, everyone rushes the original library at once.
system-design/caching-without-stampedes.i: I choose cache patterns, set TTLs with jitter and prevent stampedes and cold-start overload.

system-design/queues-retries-and-idempot.s: A retry is knocking again on a door; idempotency makes sure a second knock does not order a second pizza.
system-design/queues-retries-and-idempot.i: I set timeouts, retries and backoff safely and make repeated operations harmless with idempotency keys.

system-design/consistency-and-availabili.s: When two copies of a notebook disagree, you either wait to compare them or answer from the one you hold; each choice has a price.
system-design/consistency-and-availabili.i: I choose a consistency level per feature and handle replication lag and failover trade-offs.

system-design/quorum-leaders-and-split-b.s: A vote needs more than half the room, or two rooms could each elect a different chair.
system-design/quorum-leaders-and-split-b.i: I explain quorum, leader election, split brain and fencing, and I can operate a consensus store.

system-design/clocks-time-and-ordering.s: Two watches never agree exactly, so you order events by who told whom, not by the time on the wall.
system-design/clocks-time-and-ordering.i: I avoid wall-clock ordering, use monotonic time for durations and plan for leap seconds and clock jumps.

system-design/failure-domains-cells-and-.s: A ship is divided into watertight compartments so one hole does not sink the whole vessel.
system-design/failure-domains-cells-and-.i: I identify failure domains and use cells and bulkheads so one fault reaches only a bounded share.

system-design/blast-radius-and-shuffle-s.s: Give each customer a random few lanes of a motorway; one crash blocks only the lanes it sits in.
system-design/blast-radius-and-shuffle-s.i: I measure blast radius and use staged rollout, quotas and shuffle sharding to contain faults.

system-design/graceful-degradation-and-c.s: A tripped fuse stops the fire spreading; the house keeps its lights even if the toaster circuit is off.
system-design/graceful-degradation-and-c.i: I plan fallbacks, set circuit breakers and keep health checks about the instance itself.

system-design/rate-limiting-and-load-she.s: A restaurant that seats everyone serves nobody; a host who turns some away keeps every served table happy.
system-design/rate-limiting-and-load-she.i: I limit, shed and admit load by priority and tell clients how to back off.

system-design/multi-region-and-global-tr.s: A second office only helps if the staff can really work there and the road to it is not the road that is closed.
system-design/multi-region-and-global-tr.i: I map RTO and RPO to a multi-region pattern and steer traffic without a single point of failure.

system-design/config-and-control-plane-c.s: Changing a setting everywhere at once is like repainting every road sign overnight; stage it, and keep the old signs.
system-design/config-and-control-plane-c.i: I treat configuration as code with validation, staging, fail-static loading and rollback.

system-design/hidden-dependencies-and-si.s: The map shows the roads you use to drive; it forgets the road you use to reach the garage.
system-design/hidden-dependencies-and-si.i: I map serving, build, operate and recover dependencies and keep recovery tools independent.

system-design/worked-design-global-api-a.s: Four nines is a budget of minutes; every design choice either spends it or protects it.
system-design/worked-design-global-api-a.i: I compose cells, regions, limits and staged rollout into a design that fits a four-nines budget.

system-design/worked-design-the-status-p.s: The fire alarm must not run on the same wire as the fire.
system-design/worked-design-the-status-p.i: I design an independent communication path and run a before and after design review of an outage.

system-design/partitioning-sharding-and-.s: Cutting a library into rooms: each book belongs to one room, and adding a room should not make you move every book.
system-design/partitioning-sharding-and-.i: I choose partition keys, avoid hot keys and use consistent hashing so growth moves little data.

system-design/storage-engines-and-replic.s: A notebook you rewrite in place versus a diary you only append to and tidy later; each needs a different kind of housekeeping.
system-design/storage-engines-and-replic.i: I compare B-tree and LSM engines, choose a replication topology and watch background cleanup and metadata growth.

system-design/backup-restore-and-object-.s: A spare key kept in the same drawer as the first key is not a spare; you only know it works when you have opened the door with it.
system-design/backup-restore-and-object-.i: I design backups from RPO and RTO, keep copies independent, test timed restores and use object storage features properly.

system-design/observability-by-design.s: Fitting a car with gauges at the factory beats guessing what is wrong from the noise it makes on the motorway.
system-design/observability-by-design.i: I design SLIs, signals and traces into a system and keep monitoring independent of what it watches.

system-design/security-and-identity-by-d.s: A building with a master key for every door means one lost key opens everything; separate keys limit what a thief gets.
system-design/security-and-identity-by-d.i: I design trust boundaries, least privilege and short-lived credentials so one compromise reaches little.

system-design/capacity-planning-and-cost.s: Keeping spare seats on the train is a cost you pay so that one broken carriage does not strand the passengers.
system-design/capacity-planning-and-cost.i: I plan capacity from measurements with zone-loss headroom and make cost trade-offs explicit.

system-design/worked-design-a-url-shorte.s: A phone book where most people only ever look up the same few numbers; cache those and make the rest cheap.
system-design/worked-design-a-url-shorte.i: I design a read-heavy shortener with key generation, caching, hot links and abuse controls.

system-design/worked-design-a-rate-limit.s: A doorman who must never lock the building because his notebook is lost.
system-design/worked-design-a-rate-limit.i: I design a gateway rate limiter with local allowances, safe failure behaviour and a client contract.

system-design/worked-design-a-notificati.s: A post office sorts urgent mail into its own fast lane so a mass mailing cannot delay a telegram.
system-design/worked-design-a-notificati.i: I design fan-out with priority lanes, provider limits, deduplication and retry budgets.

system-design/worked-design-a-metrics-an.s: A river with a reservoir: it takes the flood so the town downstream stays dry, and it must never be the thing that floods.
system-design/worked-design-a-metrics-an.i: I design a telemetry pipeline with buffering, cardinality limits, tiered retention and independent alerting.

system-design/worked-design-a-multi-tena.s: An apartment block: shared plumbing needs rules and fuses so one tenant's flood does not reach the others.
system-design/worked-design-a-multi-tena.i: I design a multi-tenant platform with tenancy tiers, quotas, staged upgrades and add-on dependency reviews.

system-design/worked-design-an-authorita.s: The directory every other directory depends on must keep a printed copy so it can answer when its own office is shut.
system-design/worked-design-an-authorita.i: I design an authoritative DNS service with anycast, static stability, safe zone change and independent providers.

mlops/what-mlops-is-and-how-ml-systems-f.s: A chef who tastes every dish can notice a bad batch. A model needs the same tasting step after it ships, because it can go wrong without any alarm sounding.
mlops/what-mlops-is-and-how-ml-systems-f.i: I treat the model as one part of a system. I version data, features and models, check inputs in production, and watch prediction quality, not only latency and errors.

mlops/data-and-feature-pipelines-for-ml.s: Cooking from a recipe only works if the ingredients are what the recipe expects. Checking the ingredients before you start saves you from throwing away the whole meal.
mlops/data-and-feature-pipelines-for-ml.i: I validate every batch against a schema and expectations, version datasets so models are reproducible, use point-in-time joins to avoid leakage, and compute each feature once for training and serving.

mlops/experiment-tracking-and-reproducib.s: A cook who writes down every change can make the best cake again. Without notes, even a great cake cannot be repeated.
mlops/experiment-tracking-and-reproducib.i: I log code version, data version, parameters, seed, environment and metrics for every run, compare on a fixed evaluation set, and package training in a container so any model can be rebuilt.

mlops/training-pipelines-and-testing-mod.s: A factory checks each batch against a quality standard before shipping. A training pipeline does the same for models, so a bad batch never leaves the building.
mlops/training-pipelines-and-testing-mod.i: I automate training as staged pipeline jobs in containers, test code, data and model quality in CI, and use a gate that compares a candidate with production, including key groups, before registering it.

mlops/model-registry-packaging-and-safe-.s: A shop tests a new recipe on a few customers before changing the whole menu, and keeps the old recipe card ready in case the new one disappoints.
mlops/model-registry-packaging-and-safe-.i: I register models with lineage and stages, package them in pinned containers recorded by digest, release through shadow and canary steps with quality checks, and keep the previous version ready to roll back.

mlops/serving-models-batch-online-and-st.s: A bakery can bake bread overnight for the morning, or toast a slice to order. Batch is the overnight bake and online is the toaster. Each suits a different customer.
mlops/serving-models-batch-online-and-st.i: I pick batch, online or streaming from freshness needs, size the service with dynamic batching and readiness probes, scale on load signals, and add timeouts, concurrency limits and fallbacks.

mlops/monitoring-drift-and-retraining.s: A map goes out of date as roads change. Checking it against the real streets every so often tells you when it is time to redraw it.
mlops/monitoring-drift-and-retraining.i: I monitor input and prediction drift as early signals, measure quality as labels arrive, compare with a baseline, alert on sustained shifts, and retrain through the same gated pipeline.

aiops/what-aiops-is-and-is-not.s: A smoke alarm that goes off at every piece of toast gets its battery removed. Helpful operations tools must be right often enough that people keep listening to them.
aiops/what-aiops-is-and-is-not.i: I define the problem and a baseline first, make sure telemetry and change data are sound, trial a tool beside current practice, and keep it only if alert noise and time to cause improve.

aiops/anomaly-detection-on-metrics.s: A shop knows Saturday is busy. It does not call it a crisis when the queue is long on Saturday, only when Tuesday looks like Saturday.
aiops/anomaly-detection-on-metrics.i: I use seasonal baselines, comparing with the same time on earlier weeks, require sustained deviations, apply minimum sizes, and review each false alarm to tune or remove the rule.

aiops/alert-correlation-and-noise-reduct.s: When a power cut hits a street, you need one note saying the power is out, not a hundred notes saying every light is off.
aiops/alert-correlation-and-noise-reduct.i: I give alerts stable labels, deduplicate and group them, use dependency data to show the likely source, add careful inhibition, and measure alerts per incident to keep noise falling.

aiops/logs-and-traces-finding-patterns-w.s: Imagine sorting thousands of letters into piles by what they say. A new pile that did not exist yesterday is the first thing worth reading.
aiops/logs-and-traces-finding-patterns-w.i: I turn logs into templates, list new and fast-growing ones after a change, split counts by version and host, use traces to find slow or changed paths, and overlay the change log.

aiops/root-cause-hints-and-incident-assi.s: A detective lists everything that changed just before the crime and checks each clue. A good tool is a helper that lays out the list, not one that names the culprit alone.
aiops/root-cause-hints-and-incident-assi.i: I start from the change list and dependency health, rank hints with evidence and timing, use language models only for summaries and search with sources, and keep humans approving every production action.

aiops/safe-automation-and-auto-remediati.s: A thermostat that turns on the heating is useful. One without limits that never switches off would be a danger, so every automatic helper needs a stop.
aiops/safe-automation-and-auto-remediati.i: I automate frequent, low-risk, verifiable fixes with preconditions, action limits, cooldowns, a verify step, audit logging and a kill switch, and move from suggestion to approval to unattended gradually.

system-design/worked-design-a-chat-and-m.s: A postal sorting office needs every letter to reach the right person, in order, even if a van breaks down. Chat works the same way, with acknowledgements as signed receipts.
system-design/worked-design-a-chat-and-m.i: I size chat by connections and message rate, partition by conversation for ordering, use client message ids for idempotency, drive delivery with acknowledgements and plan for reconnect storms.

system-design/worked-design-a-news-feed-.s: A newspaper can deliver each edition to every doorstep in advance, or let readers pick up the paper on demand. For a few famous writers the second is easier.
system-design/worked-design-a-news-feed-.i: I use write fan-out for normal accounts, read-time merge for very popular ones, rank a short candidate list with a timeout and chronological fallback, and filter deletes at read time.

system-design/worked-design-video-upload.s: A video service is a factory: raw film arrives, workers cut it into standard sizes, and trucks deliver copies to local shops so the customer never travels to the factory.
system-design/worked-design-video-upload.i: I use chunked resumable uploads, a queue of idempotent transcode jobs with timeouts, retry limits and a dead-letter queue, tiered storage and a CDN with a purge path.

system-design/worked-design-a-distribute.s: Three friends each keep a copy of the address book. A change counts once two of them have written it, so a read from any two will see the newest page.
system-design/worked-design-a-distribute.i: I use a hash ring with virtual nodes, three replicas across zones, quorum reads and writes with R + W > N, hinted handoff and anti-entropy, and an explicit conflict rule.

system-design/worked-design-a-payments-l.s: A careful shopkeeper writes every sale in a book in ink, never erasing, and checks the till against the book each night. A ledger works the same way.
system-design/worked-design-a-payments-l.i: I use immutable double-entry records, idempotency keys stored in the same transaction, a payment state machine, treat processor timeouts as unknown, and reconcile daily.

system-design/worked-design-search-autoc.s: A helpful shop assistant guesses the rest of your sentence from the first few letters, using the most popular requests. If they are away, you can still ask for what you want yourself.
system-design/worked-design-search-autoc.i: I hold a prefix to top-ten map in memory, cache at the edge, debounce on the client, rebuild the index offline with validation and staged rollout, filter with a blocklist and degrade to no suggestions.

mlops/debugging-ml-systems-in-production.s: A shop sells less. Before changing the menu, check the doors, the lights and the prices. Most problems are there, not in the recipes.
mlops/debugging-ml-systems-in-production.i: I check what changed, then data, then features against training, replay a logged bad prediction, and only then look at the model and serving, one layer at a time.

aiops/debugging-and-investigating-aiops-.s: A friend guesses why the car will not start. Good guess, but you still look at the fuel gauge before calling a tow truck.
aiops/debugging-and-investigating-aiops-.i: I treat AI output as a hypothesis: ask for evidence, test it against metrics and the timeline, keep a person approving actions, and record hits and misses.

virtualization/what-virtualization-is-an.s: Virtualization lets one physical server run several separate virtual computers, so hardware is not wasted on one small job. A hypervisor is the program that keeps them apart.
virtualization/what-virtualization-is-an.i: A hypervisor shares one machine between many guests. KVM turns Linux into one, QEMU emulates the devices, libvirt manages them, and virtio drivers keep disk and network fast. Always check that hardware virtualization is on.

virtualization/cpu-memory-and-overcommit.s: A host can promise more CPU than it has, because guests seldom all work at once. The risk is that on a busy day they all wait, and you see it as steal time.
virtualization/cpu-memory-and-overcommit.i: vCPUs are host threads, memory is the tighter limit. Watch steal or ready time on CPU and any host swap on memory. Keep production databases near 1 to 1 and pin big guests to one NUMA node.

virtualization/virtual-disks-snapshots-a.s: A virtual machine's disk is a file. Thin files only grow as needed, and a snapshot starts a new file for later changes. Too many snapshots fill the storage.
virtualization/virtual-disks-snapshots-a.i: Disks are raw or qcow2 files. Thin provisioning saves space but overcommits storage. Snapshots add delta layers, so keep them short-lived, never treat them as backups, and alert on pool free space.

virtualization/virtual-networking-bridge.s: A virtual machine plugs into a virtual switch. If the switch is set up wrongly, the machine has a cable but cannot reach anyone.
virtualization/virtual-networking-bridge.i: Guests attach to bridges. Choose bridged for servers, NAT for tests. VLAN tags must be allowed on the uplink trunk. SR-IOV trades flexibility for speed.

virtualization/live-migration-ha-and-tro.s: Live migration moves a running machine to another server without stopping it. High availability restarts machines on another server if one breaks.
virtualization/live-migration-ha-and-tro.i: Live migration needs shared or copied storage, compatible CPUs and a fast network. HA needs fencing and quorum to avoid split brain. Plan N+1 capacity so a failed host's guests have somewhere to run.

storage/block-file-and-object-storage.s: Storage comes in three kinds: a raw disk, shared folders, and an object store you reach over the web. Each is good at different jobs.
storage/block-file-and-object-storage.i: Choose block, file or object by access pattern. Judge a disk by IOPS, throughput and latency, not only capacity. Measure with iostat and fio, and know a cloud volume's baseline and burst.

storage/filesystems-ext4-xfs-and-mounts.s: A filesystem is the filing system on a disk. The most important job is mounting it the same way every boot, so the server always finds its data.
storage/filesystems-ext4-xfs-and-mounts.i: Know ext4 and XFS. Mount by UUID, add nofail on data disks, and test every fstab change with mount -a. Check df -i as well as df -h when writes fail.

storage/lvm-and-raid.s: LVM lets you add space to a volume while the server runs. RAID lets a disk break without losing data. Neither replaces a backup.
storage/lvm-and-raid.i: LVM stacks PV, VG and LV so volumes can grow online; remember the filesystem must grow as well. RAID gives redundancy, not backup. Alert on degraded arrays and prefer RAID 6 or 10 for big disks.

storage/network-storage-nfs-iscsi-and-ce.s: Network storage lets many servers use the same data. If the network or storage server stops, everything that uses it can stop too.
storage/network-storage-nfs-iscsi-and-ce.i: NFS shares files, iSCSI shares disks, Ceph spreads copies across servers. Use hard mounts for data, keep user IDs aligned, give iSCSI its own network with multipath, and keep Ceph below 85 percent full.

storage/performance-backups-and-troubles.s: A disk can be slow, full, or gone. First find out which. A full disk is sometimes full of a file you cannot see, because a program is still holding it open.
storage/performance-backups-and-troubles.i: Use iostat to find slow disks and df, du and lsof +L1 to find what fills a disk. Back up with the 3-2-1 rule, define RPO and RTO, and test restores.

sql-ops/reading-explain-and-finding-slow.s: When a database is slow, a few queries are usually to blame. EXPLAIN shows how the database runs one, so you can see whether it reads far too much.
sql-ops/reading-explain-and-finding-slow.i: Rank queries by total time with pg_stat_statements, then read EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Look for seq scans on big tables, estimate versus actual rows, and spilled sorts. Change one thing and compare.

sql-ops/indexes-that-help-and-indexes-th.s: An index is like the index of a book: it makes looking things up fast. But it must be updated whenever the book changes, so having too many slows writing.
sql-ops/indexes-that-help-and-indexes-th.i: Design composite indexes with equality columns first, use partial and covering indexes where they fit, and review pg_stat_user_indexes for unused or duplicate indexes. Each index costs write speed.

sql-ops/locks-deadlocks-and-long-transac.s: Sometimes a query is slow because it is waiting for another one to finish. A forgotten open transaction can hold up everyone behind it.
sql-ops/locks-deadlocks-and-long-transac.i: Find blockers with pg_stat_activity and pg_blocking_pids. Keep transactions short, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and lock_timeout, fix deadlocks by consistent lock order and retries.

sql-ops/connections-pooling-and-capacity.s: A database can only handle so many connections. If every copy of the application opens many, the limit is reached quickly and new users are refused.
sql-ops/connections-pooling-and-capacity.i: Add up instances times pool size for every client. Use PgBouncer in transaction mode to multiplex clients, keep work_mem modest and raise it per job, and reserve connections for administrators.

sql-ops/replication-lag-vacuum-and-day-t.s: A database needs regular care: copies must stay up to date, old data must be cleaned out, and backups must really work.
sql-ops/replication-lag-vacuum-and-day-t.i: Monitor replication lag and slots, tune autovacuum for big tables, change schemas with CONCURRENTLY and short locks, and keep tested backups with WAL for point-in-time recovery.

gpu-serving/gpu-basics-memory-and-what-l.s: A big language model has to fit in the graphics card's memory, and it also needs memory for every conversation it is handling. Memory runs out before anything else.
gpu-serving/gpu-basics-memory-and-what-l.i: Estimate memory as weights plus KV cache at peak load. Decode speed is bound by memory bandwidth, so batching and quantization raise throughput. Test quality when you compress.

gpu-serving/serving-stacks-vllm-tgi-trit.s: A serving engine keeps the graphics card busy by mixing many users' requests together. It is the difference between one user and many users on the same hardware.
gpu-serving/serving-stacks-vllm-tgi-trit.i: Use an engine with continuous batching and paged cache, such as vLLM or TGI. Tune max-model-len, GPU memory utilization and parallelism, read the KV cache size at start-up, and cache weights on a volume.

gpu-serving/gpus-on-kubernetes.s: Kubernetes treats a graphics card as a unit it hands to one pod at a time. Pods that ask for one wait until a card is free.
gpu-serving/gpus-on-kubernetes.i: Install the driver, runtime hook and device plugin. Request nvidia.com/gpu in limits as a whole number, taint GPU nodes, and read FailedScheduling messages. Use MIG for isolation and plan node shapes for multi-GPU jobs.

gpu-serving/scaling-latency-and-cost.s: Users care how soon text starts and how fast it flows. Servers cost money all the time, so scale up when people wait and not when the CPU looks busy.
gpu-serving/scaling-latency-and-cost.i: Track TTFT, token speed and percentiles. Scale on waiting requests or cache use, not CPU. Cost per token is GPU price divided by tokens produced, so utilisation drives it.

gpu-serving/monitoring-and-debugging-gpu.s: When a graphics card job misbehaves, look at the card itself: how full its memory is, how hot it is, and whether its drivers report errors.
gpu-serving/monitoring-and-debugging-gpu.i: Use nvidia-smi and DCGM metrics. Look for memory exhaustion, throttling, XID and ECC errors, and hung collective operations. Do not treat GPU-Util as useful work.

openstack/what-openstack-is-and-core-ser.s: OpenStack is a set of programs that turn many ordinary servers into a private cloud. Each program does one job, such as machines, networks or disks.
openstack/what-openstack-is-and-core-ser.i: OpenStack is a private cloud built from services: Keystone for identity, Nova for compute, Neutron for networks, Glance for images, Cinder for disks. All depend on a database and a message queue.

openstack/identity-projects-quotas-and-k.s: Before you can create anything, OpenStack asks who you are and which project the work belongs to. Each project has limits, called quotas.
openstack/identity-projects-quotas-and-k.i: Keystone gives users roles on projects and issues tokens. Projects have quotas. 401 means authentication, 403 means policy. Use application credentials for automation.

openstack/compute-flavors-images-and-sch.s: To create a server, OpenStack has to find a machine with enough free room. If none has, the new server ends up in an error state.
openstack/compute-flavors-images-and-sch.i: Flavor plus image plus network makes a server. The scheduler and Placement pick a node. No valid host means no node passed every check: look at service state, free resources per node, aggregates and the scheduler log.

openstack/neutron-networking-security-gr.s: Neutron gives each team its own virtual networks and firewalls. If you cannot reach a server, it is often a firewall rule or a missing public address.
openstack/neutron-networking-security-gr.i: Neutron provides networks, subnets, ports and routers. Security groups only allow, floating IPs map public to private addresses. Debug from the inside out: boot log, port, security group, floating IP, router, service.

openstack/operating-openstack-logs-upgra.s: Running a private cloud means knowing where each part writes its log and how to tell when the shared pieces are unhealthy.
openstack/operating-openstack-logs-upgra.i: Follow the request id through the logs, check agents, queues and the database first, and reset stuck states only after comparing with the hypervisor. Back up before upgrades and keep headroom for host failure.

baremetal/servers-racks-and-remote-manag.s: A rack server is a normal computer in a flat box, with a small second computer inside that lets you switch it on, off and watch it from far away.
baremetal/servers-racks-and-remote-manag.i: Rack servers are limited by power and cooling more than space. The BMC, reached with IPMI or Redfish, manages power, console and the event log even when the host is dead.

baremetal/provisioning-pxe-dhcp-and-imag.s: A new server has nothing on its disks, so it asks the network for help, and the network tells it where to find an installer and an answer sheet.
baremetal/provisioning-pxe-dhcp-and-imag.i: PXE boot is a chain: DHCP gives an address and the boot file location, TFTP or HTTP delivers the loader, and an installer reads an answer file. Image based tools like MAAS and Ironic make it repeatable.

baremetal/disks-raid-firmware-and-burn-i.s: Disks wear out. RAID keeps a server running when one fails, and tests on new machines find weak parts before they hold anything important.
baremetal/disks-raid-firmware-and-burn-i.i: RAID protects against disk failure but is not a backup. A degraded array is urgent until rebuilt. SMART and burn-in find bad drives and memory before they cause an outage.

baremetal/datacenter-networking-leaf-spi.s: Racks connect through switches arranged so that any server reaches any other in a few hops, and each server uses two cables so one can fail.
baremetal/datacenter-networking-leaf-spi.i: Leaf-spine fabrics give predictable paths for east-west traffic. Bonds join links; LACP needs both ends configured. Management traffic belongs on its own network.

baremetal/operating-a-fleet-failures-lif.s: When you own hundreds of machines, some part fails every week, so you need a routine for finding which part and replacing it safely.
baremetal/operating-a-fleet-failures-lif.i: Read the BMC event log, SMART and counters before replacing anything. Drain, repair one thing, test, record. Plan spares, wipe retired disks, and roll out firmware in waves.

service-mesh/kubernetes-networking-under.s: Every pod gets its own address, and a Service is a steady name and address that passes traffic to whichever pods are alive right now.
service-mesh/kubernetes-networking-under.i: The CNI gives pods addresses and routes. Services use selectors to find endpoints, kube-proxy to forward, and CoreDNS to name them. Ingress and Gateway bring outside traffic in.

service-mesh/cni-network-policy-and-ebpf.s: By default every pod can call every other pod. A network policy is a list of who is allowed in or out, and the network plugin has to enforce it.
service-mesh/cni-network-policy-and-ebpf.i: NetworkPolicy is additive and default-open until a pod is selected. The CNI must enforce it. eBPF in Cilium enforces by identity and replaces long iptables chains.

service-mesh/what-a-service-mesh-is-and-.s: A service mesh puts a helper beside every service that handles the network chores the same way for all of them, so teams do not each have to write them.
service-mesh/what-a-service-mesh-is-and-.i: A mesh has a data plane of proxies and a control plane that configures them and issues certificates. Sidecars are simple but costly; ambient lowers the cost. Use one for a clear need.

service-mesh/mtls-and-traffic-management.s: The mesh can make every call private and checked, and send a small slice of traffic to a new version, just by changing configuration.
service-mesh/mtls-and-traffic-management.i: mTLS uses workload identity and rotating certificates. PeerAuthentication sets the mode. VirtualService routes, DestinationRule defines subsets. Retries and timeouts need care to avoid storms.

service-mesh/observing-and-troubleshooti.s: The helper beside each service writes down every call it sees, so you can tell which hop failed and why.
service-mesh/observing-and-troubleshooti.i: Use proxy-status to check config sync, analyze to check configuration, and response flags in proxy logs to place the failure. Follow a fixed method before changing anything.

linux/troubleshooting-playbook-method-an.s: A doctor asks questions and takes vital signs before prescribing anything. Troubleshooting a server works the same way: look first, then act.
linux/troubleshooting-playbook-method-an.i: I ask what changed and who is affected, then apply the USE method to CPU, memory, disk and network, checking dmesg, vmstat, iostat and ss before I change one thing at a time.

linux/troubleshooting-playbook-high-load.s: Load average is like the queue at a bank: it counts people waiting and people being served, not just how busy the tellers are.
linux/troubleshooting-playbook-high-load.i: I compare load with the core count, split CPU time into user, system, iowait and steal, find the busy thread with top -H or pidstat, and only then decide to fix, limit or scale.

linux/troubleshooting-playbook-memory-pr.s: Linux uses spare memory as a desk for papers it might need again. A full desk is normal; a desk with no room to work is the problem.
linux/troubleshooting-playbook-memory-pr.i: I read the available figure, not free, check vmstat for swap in and out, and look in dmesg or the journal for OOM kills. For containers I compare the working set with the cgroup limit.

linux/troubleshooting-playbook-disk-full.s: A disk can be full of space or full of name tags. Many tiny files can use up all the labels even when the shelves still have room.
linux/troubleshooting-playbook-disk-full.i: I check df for space and df -i for inodes, use du with -x to find big directories, look for deleted-but-open files with lsof +L1, and read iostat await and queue size for slow disks.

linux/troubleshooting-playbook-network-d.s: When a parcel is late, you check each stage: the van, the sorting depot, the street address. Check a network path layer by layer in the same way.
linux/troubleshooting-playbook-network-d.i: I check interface errors with ip -s link and ethtool, retransmits with nstat and ss -ti, path MTU with a do-not-fragment ping, and time DNS, connect and TLS separately with curl.

linux/troubleshooting-playbook-boot-fail.s: A reboot is a stress test of every promise you made to the system. Things you forgot about show up when the power comes back.
linux/troubleshooting-playbook-boot-fail.i: I read systemctl status and the full journalctl for the boot, use systemd-analyze blame and critical-chain for slow starts, and fix fstab with UUIDs and nofail when a mount drops the system into emergency mode.

python/sre-automation-aws-with-boto3-saf.s: A script that can delete cloud resources is like a power tool: safe habits matter more than speed. Read the label, test on scrap, then cut.
python/sre-automation-aws-with-boto3-saf.i: I use named profiles or assumed roles, set the region explicitly, paginate every list call, select by tags, default to a dry run with an explicit apply flag, and print the caller identity first.

python/sre-automation-kubernetes-client-.s: kubectl is for people reading a screen. The Python client is for programs that need facts in a form they can count and compare.
python/sre-automation-kubernetes-client-.i: I load the in-cluster or kubeconfig credentials, list pods with paging, read container statuses and resource settings as objects, and use a read-only service account that handles 403, 404 and 429 errors.

python/sre-automation-retries-backoff-ti.s: If you knock and nobody answers, you wait a bit longer each time, not hammer the door. Machines should behave the same way, with a limit.
python/sre-automation-retries-backoff-ti.i: I set connect and read timeouts on every call, retry only transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter, honor Retry-After, cap attempts and time, and make writes idempotent with keys or existence checks.

python/sre-automation-parsing-logs-and-b.s: A detective lines up witness statements by time. A timeline script does the same with logs from many systems.
python/sre-automation-parsing-logs-and-b.i: I parse lines defensively, count the ones that fail, group messages by replacing ids with placeholders, stream large files, convert every timestamp to UTC and merge sources into one sorted list.

python/sre-automation-chatops-alert-hand.s: A chat bot with a button that restarts servers is useful and dangerous, like giving a stranger a key. Check who they are and what they may open.
python/sre-automation-chatops-alert-hand.i: I verify webhook signatures with an HMAC and constant-time comparison, deduplicate by fingerprint, post structured messages with links, and allow only approved actions with approvals and an audit line.

python/sre-automation-safe-bulk-operatio.s: Painting one room is a chore. Painting every room in a hotel needs a plan, a test patch and a way to stop when the colour is wrong.
python/sre-automation-safe-bulk-operatio.i: I separate the plan from the apply, review the list, start with a canary, work in batches with a health check and rate limits, keep a kill switch, store state to resume and write an audit log.

networking/dns-tls-pki-dns-records-resol.s: DNS is a phone book that everyone photocopies. The original is correct, but old copies stay in drawers until they expire.
networking/dns-tls-pki-dns-records-resol.i: I explain stub, recursive and authoritative servers, the main record types, why a CNAME cannot sit at the apex, how TTL and negative caching work, and I query the authoritative server with dig when I suspect stale answers.

networking/dns-tls-pki-debugging-dns-fai.s: When a letter does not arrive, you check whether the address exists, whether the post office is open and whether your own mailbox is the problem.
networking/dns-tls-pki-debugging-dns-fai.i: I read the dig status (NOERROR, NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, timeout), test the host's own resolver path with getent, then a public resolver, then the authoritative server, and I check search domains and ndots in containers.

networking/dns-tls-pki-tls-handshake-and.s: A certificate chain is a chain of introductions: someone you trust vouches for someone who vouches for the server you want to talk to.
networking/dns-tls-pki-tls-handshake-and.i: I describe the TLS 1.3 handshake and SNI, explain leaf, intermediate and root certificates, check names against the SAN list and use openssl s_client with -servername to show the chain, dates and verify result.

networking/dns-tls-pki-certificate-lifec.s: A passport expires so that a lost one stops working. Certificates expire for the same reason, and need renewing before a trip, not at the airport.
networking/dns-tls-pki-certificate-lifec.i: I generate a key and CSR, prove control with ACME HTTP-01 or DNS-01, automate renewal with a client, reload the service after renewal, and alert on probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry before the dates matter.

networking/dns-tls-pki-mtls-and-internal.s: mTLS is a door where both sides show ID. The guard checks you and you check the guard, so neither side has to take the other's word.
networking/dns-tls-pki-mtls-and-internal.i: I use an offline root with online intermediates, short-lived workload certificates, cert-manager to issue and renew them, a SPIFFE-style identity in the SAN, and trust bundles that overlap during a CA rotation.

networking/dns-tls-pki-outage-prevention.s: Most house fires start with something small and ignored. Most DNS and certificate outages do too: an expiry date nobody wrote down.
networking/dns-tls-pki-outage-prevention.i: I keep a generated inventory of domains, zones and certificates, alert on certificate, CA and domain expiry, change DNS through code with review and a rollback, test targets with curl --resolve and use two DNS providers for critical names.

cloud/finops-reading-a-cloud-bill-and-ta.s: A cloud bill is a till receipt with thousands of lines. Tags are the labels that tell you which team's shopping each line belongs to.
cloud/finops-reading-a-cloud-bill-and-ta.i: I group cost by service, account, region and tag, look at daily trends to date a jump, enforce a small set of mandatory tags, and track unit cost such as cost per order, not only the total.

cloud/finops-rightsizing-and-removing-wa.s: Paying for an idle server is like heating an empty house. First find which rooms nobody uses, then turn the heat down.
cloud/finops-rightsizing-and-removing-wa.i: I rightsize from high-percentile utilization over a representative period, find unattached volumes, old snapshots and idle load balancers, schedule non-production environments off hours and delete with a grace period and owner check.

cloud/finops-commitments-savings-plans-a.s: Buying a monthly train pass is cheaper than single tickets only if you ride every day. Commit to the trips you always make.
cloud/finops-commitments-savings-plans-a.i: I commit to the always-on baseline in steps, track coverage and utilization, stagger expiry dates, run fault-tolerant work on spot with interruption handling and keep stateful systems on stable capacity.

cloud/finops-kubernetes-cost-allocation-.s: On a shared bus you pay for the seats you reserved, not the seats you sat in. Pods reserve CPU and memory the same way.
cloud/finops-kubernetes-cost-allocation-.i: I compare requests with real usage, set requests from a long window with headroom, use VPA recommendations and HPA, apply quotas per namespace and allocate node cost to teams by labels with idle cost shown separately.

cloud/finops-data-transfer-storage-and-h.s: The price tag on the shelf is not the whole cost: delivery, packaging and storage add up. In the cloud the delivery is data transfer.
cloud/finops-data-transfer-storage-and-h.i: I look at egress, cross-zone and cross-region traffic, NAT gateway processing, storage class and lifecycle rules, and observability ingest and cardinality, and I use private endpoints and caches to cut the biggest flows.

cloud/finops-budgets-anomalies-and-a-cos.s: A smoke alarm beats checking the kitchen every hour. Budgets and anomaly alerts watch the bill for you and tell the right person.
cloud/finops-budgets-anomalies-and-a-cos.i: I set actual and forecast budget alerts, add anomaly detection routed to owning teams, run a weekly and monthly review with owned actions, and put a cost section and an estimate into design reviews and pull requests.

storage/backup-and-dr-strategy-3-2-1-and.s: A spare key kept in the same drawer as the first key is not a spare. Backups must live somewhere a single accident cannot reach.
storage/backup-and-dr-strategy-3-2-1-and.i: I start from RPO and RTO, apply 3-2-1 with an immutable or offline copy, choose full, incremental and snapshot methods, set retention, encrypt, and back up configuration and keys as well as data.

storage/backup-and-dr-database-backups-a.s: A base backup is a photo of the library; the archived log is the diary of every book moved since. Together you can rebuild any day.
storage/backup-and-dr-database-backups-a.i: I take physical base backups with continuous WAL archiving using pgBackRest or Barman, use pg_dump for portable exports, restore to a new server to a chosen time, and alert on archive failures and backup age.

storage/backup-and-dr-kubernetes-etcd-an.s: Rebuilding a cluster is like rebuilding a house from blueprints: the plans are in version control, and only the furniture, your data, needs a backup.
storage/backup-and-dr-kubernetes-etcd-an.i: I keep manifests and infrastructure code in version control, snapshot etcd on a schedule and copy it off the node encrypted, use CSI volume snapshots with a hook for consistency, and back up databases with their own tools.

storage/backup-and-dr-testing-restores-a.s: A fire extinguisher nobody has tested is just a red decoration. A backup nobody has restored is the same.
storage/backup-and-dr-testing-restores-a.i: I verify at three levels: the job succeeded, the data passes integrity checks, and a scheduled automated restore into a clean environment passes application-level checks. I track restore time against RTO.

storage/backup-and-dr-disaster-recovery-.s: A spare tyre, a second car, or two cars always on the road: DR patterns trade money for how quickly you can keep going.
storage/backup-and-dr-disaster-recovery-.i: I compare backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active against RTO and RPO, plan data replication and consistency, design traffic failover, define who decides, and rehearse failover and failback.

storage/backup-and-dr-ransomware-immutab.s: Keep one copy of your valuables in a safe that even you cannot open before the timer ends. That is what immutable backups do.
storage/backup-and-dr-ransomware-immutab.i: I use object lock or offline copies, a separate account with a write-only path, versioning and long retention, alerts on deletes, and a runbook that starts with containment and restores in dependency order.

virtualization/virtualization-ops-capaci.s: A hotel sells more rooms than it has guests who actually show up. It works until everyone arrives at once, which is contention.
virtualization/virtualization-ops-capaci.i: I use modest overcommit ratios, higher for CPU and low for memory, watch steal, ballooning, swap and I/O wait, use NUMA-aware placement for demanding guests and separate pools and limits to contain noisy neighbours.

virtualization/virtualization-ops-libvir.s: Running a host is like running an airport: the planes land all day, and maintenance has to happen without stopping the flights.
virtualization/virtualization-ops-libvir.i: I manage guests with virsh and the domain XML, use --live and --config correctly, take short-lived quiesced snapshots, patch hosts by live migrating guests away and keep host configuration identical by code.

virtualization/virtualization-ops-guest-.s: To find why a car is slow, you check the engine and the road. For a VM, look inside the guest and at the host at the same time.
virtualization/virtualization-ops-guest-.i: I define the symptom, check USE signals in the guest, compare with host-side counters from virsh domstats, iostat and virt-top, look at storage and network paths, and verify virtio drivers and guest agents.

openstack/openstack-ops-no-valid-host-an.s: No valid host is like a restaurant saying it has no table. It could be full, closed, or have no table for your party size.
openstack/openstack-ops-no-valid-host-an.i: I read the instance fault and request ID, query Placement with allocation candidate list, check compute services and aggregates, and search the scheduler log for the filter that rejected hosts, including cell discovery for new nodes.

openstack/openstack-ops-neutron-and-ceph.s: Networking and storage are the roads and the warehouse of a cloud. When either jams, every service feels it.
openstack/openstack-ops-neutron-and-ceph.i: For Neutron I check agents, port binding and security groups, then trace the data path with ovs, namespaces and tcpdump at each hop and compare MTUs. For Ceph I read ceph -s, health detail, OSD tree, df and perf.

openstack/openstack-ops-maintenance-evac.s: Maintenance on a busy cloud is like changing a tyre while the car keeps rolling slowly: you need a plan, helpers and a safe order.
openstack/openstack-ops-maintenance-evac.i: I disable the compute service, check capacity, live migrate guests in batches, patch and verify, and re-enable. For a dead host I confirm it is fenced before evacuating, and I run pre-checks and a canary test around every change.

sre/senior-skills-writing-design-docs-an.s: A design document is a map you draw before the journey, so others can say there is a cliff on that route.
sre/senior-skills-writing-design-docs-an.i: I write short documents with context, goals, non-goals, a proposal, real alternatives, risks and rollout, send them early to named reviewers with a deadline, and record the decision with its status and date.

sre/senior-skills-estimating-and-plannin.s: An estimate is a weather forecast, not a promise: it says what is likely and how sure you are, and it changes as the clouds move.
sre/senior-skills-estimating-and-plannin.i: I give ranges with assumptions and risks, do a short spike to reduce uncertainty, slice work into testable pieces, tackle the riskiest part first, define done as running in production and keep slack in the plan.

sre/senior-skills-running-incident-and-p.s: A good incident call is like a good orchestra rehearsal: one conductor, clear parts and nobody playing over the others.
sre/senior-skills-running-incident-and-p.i: I name an incident commander, scribe and comms lead, set update cadence, favor mitigation over root cause, label hypotheses and then run a blameless review with a timeline and a few owned, dated actions.

sre/senior-skills-mentoring-and-growing-.s: A good mentor teaches someone to fish and then lets them cast the line, even when the mentor could catch the fish faster.
sre/senior-skills-mentoring-and-growing-.i: I agree on goals and rhythm, ask what they tried and expect, pair with them driving, delegate stretch tasks with context and checkpoints, and give specific feedback using situation, behavior, impact and next step.

sre/senior-skills-influencing-and-stakeh.s: You cannot order people you do not manage, so you earn agreement by showing them what they gain and what worries them.
sre/senior-skills-influencing-and-stakeh.i: I map stakeholders and their concerns, talk to them before meetings, build a case with data, options and a clear decision request, start with a pilot, decline with alternatives and share bad news early with a plan.

sre/senior-skills-interviewing-and-hirin.s: A good interview is a fair measuring tape applied the same way to everyone, not a mood ring that reflects the interviewer.
sre/senior-skills-interviewing-and-hirin.i: I define competencies and a scorecard first, ask realistic scenario questions with follow-ups, take notes, submit independent scores before the debrief, watch for bias and keep the candidate experience respectful.

cicd/how-ci-platforms-differ.s: Every CI system watches for a change, starts a job on a worker and reports pass or fail. The three platforms differ in where the config lives, who runs the workers and how much you can change.
cicd/how-ci-platforms-differ.i: All three run pipelines of jobs on runners triggered by events. Actions and GitLab CI are hosted by the forge with YAML beside the code, while Tekton is Kubernetes-native and runs as cluster resources. I pick by where code lives, who runs workers and how much customization is needed.

cicd/actions-workflows-jobs-and-steps.s: A workflow is a YAML file that says when to run and what jobs to do. Each job runs steps on a fresh machine, and you read the run log to see where it broke.
cicd/actions-workflows-jobs-and-steps.i: Workflows live in .github/workflows, are triggered by events and contain jobs that run in parallel on separate runners unless they declare needs. Steps either run shell or call actions, and step and job outputs pass values on. I scope the GITHUB_TOKEN with permissions.

cicd/actions-triggers-matrices-and-cachi.s: Triggers decide when a workflow runs. Matrices run the same job for many versions, and caches reuse downloaded files so builds finish faster.
cicd/actions-triggers-matrices-and-cachi.i: I scope on with branch and path filters, use matrix with fail-fast and include or exclude, cancel superseded runs with concurrency and cache with a key built from lockfile hashes. I avoid pull_request_target unless I understand its trust model.

cicd/actions-reusable-workflows-and-comp.s: Instead of copying the same pipeline into every repository, you write it once and call it. Reusable workflows share whole jobs, and composite actions share a few steps.
cicd/actions-reusable-workflows-and-comp.i: workflow_call workflows take inputs and secrets and are called with uses at job level, while composite actions bundle steps behind an action.yml. I pin callers to a tag or SHA, document inputs and keep secrets explicit.

cicd/actions-secrets-oidc-and-hardening.s: Workflows run code with access to secrets, so they need guarding. You keep secrets out of logs, pin third-party actions and let the cloud trust the workflow without storing a password.
cicd/actions-secrets-oidc-and-hardening.i: I use environment secrets with required reviewers, replace stored cloud keys with OIDC federation and id-token write, pin actions to SHAs, restrict token permissions and treat pull request title and branch names as untrusted input to avoid script injection.

cicd/actions-runners-environments-and-de.s: Runners are the machines that do the work and environments guard where you deploy. You pick hosted for ease or self-hosted for control, and add approvals before production.
cicd/actions-runners-environments-and-de.i: Hosted runners are ephemeral and managed, while self-hosted runners suit private networks and special hardware but need isolation and patching. Environments add reviewers, wait timers and scoped secrets, and concurrency keeps one deploy per environment. I prefer ephemeral autoscaled runners.

cicd/gitlab-ci-pipelines-stages-and-jobs.s: GitLab CI reads one file in your repository. You list stages in order, define jobs inside them and a runner executes each job in a container.
cicd/gitlab-ci-pipelines-stages-and-jobs.i: A pipeline is built from stages and jobs in .gitlab-ci.yml. Jobs in a stage run in parallel, stages run in order, and each job runs in the image I choose with script, before_script and after_script. Variables set at several levels, with the most specific winning.

cicd/gitlab-ci-rules-artifacts-and-cache.s: Rules decide which jobs run for each change, artifacts carry results to later jobs and caches save downloads. Mixing up artifacts and caches is the usual mistake.
cicd/gitlab-ci-rules-artifacts-and-cache.i: I use rules with if, changes and exists instead of only and except, workflow rules to avoid duplicate pipelines, artifacts for results between jobs and caches keyed by lockfile for dependencies. Cache is best-effort, artifacts are guaranteed.

cicd/gitlab-ci-includes-templates-and-dy.s: Large pipelines get unwieldy. You split them into files with include, reuse blocks with extends and run child pipelines for each part of a monorepo.
cicd/gitlab-ci-includes-templates-and-dy.i: I use include for local, project, remote and template files, extends and hidden jobs for reuse, trigger for parent and child pipelines and dynamic child pipelines generated from an artifact. I pin included project files to a ref.

cicd/gitlab-runners-environments-and-sec.s: A GitLab runner is the program that picks up your jobs. You choose where it runs, protect secrets with protected variables and gate production with environments.
cicd/gitlab-runners-environments-and-sec.i: Runners register to an instance, group or project and use executors such as docker or kubernetes. I tag runners, use protected and masked variables, protected branches for deploy jobs, environments with approvals and job tokens or OIDC instead of long-lived keys.

cicd/tekton-tasks-pipelines-and-workspac.s: Tekton turns CI into Kubernetes objects. A Task is a list of container steps, a Pipeline links tasks, and a run object starts them as pods.
cicd/tekton-tasks-pipelines-and-workspac.i: A Task has steps that run in one pod and share workspaces and results. A Pipeline orders tasks with runAfter and params, and TaskRun and PipelineRun instantiate them. Workspaces map to volumes, and results pass small values between tasks.

cicd/tekton-triggers-chains-and-producti.s: Tekton does not watch your repository by itself. Triggers turn webhooks into runs, Chains signs what you built and RBAC and quotas keep the cluster safe.
cicd/tekton-triggers-chains-and-producti.i: Triggers use EventListener, TriggerBinding and TriggerTemplate to create runs from events. Chains signs TaskRun results and produces provenance. In production I use dedicated service accounts, namespaces, quotas, pinned and signed task bundles, pruning and metrics.

cicd/choosing-and-migrating-between-ci-p.s: There is no best CI tool, only the best fit for your team. You compare cost, security, scale and effort, then move one pipeline at a time.
cicd/choosing-and-migrating-between-ci-p.i: I compare hosting model, runner control, ecosystem, policy and audit, cost at scale and team skills. For migration I inventory pipelines, extract logic into scripts, move a pilot, run both in parallel and compare results before cutting over.

baremetal/bmc-ipmi-and-redfish-automatio.s: Every server has a small second computer called the BMC that works even when the main system is off. You use it to power servers on and off, set boot order and read sensors from far away.
baremetal/bmc-ipmi-and-redfish-automatio.i: The BMC provides out-of-band power, console and sensor access over IPMI or the newer Redfish REST API. I keep it on an isolated management network, change default credentials, disable unused protocols and script power, boot and inventory tasks.

baremetal/cloud-init-and-first-boot-conf.s: cloud-init runs once when a machine first starts and applies settings such as users, keys and packages. It is how one generic image becomes many different servers.
baremetal/cloud-init-and-first-boot-conf.i: cloud-init reads metadata and user data from a datasource, runs modules in stages and writes logs under /var/log. I keep images generic, put identity in user data, make config idempotent and debug with cloud-init status and the logs.

baremetal/firmware-and-bios-management-a.s: Servers carry firmware in many places: BIOS, BMC, network cards and disks. You keep them on known versions and settings so machines behave the same.
baremetal/firmware-and-bios-management-a.i: I define a firmware and BIOS baseline per hardware model, read it through Redfish or vendor tools, roll updates in waves with canaries and rollback plans, and check drift regularly. Settings such as power profile and virtualization flags are part of the baseline.

baremetal/maas-and-ironic-bare-metal-pro.s: Tools like MAAS and Ironic treat physical servers like cloud machines. They discover hardware, test it and install an operating system on request through an API.
baremetal/maas-and-ironic-bare-metal-pro.i: MAAS and Ironic enroll machines through the BMC, commission them to collect hardware facts, then deploy images using PXE or virtual media with power control. I use them to get a repeatable lifecycle, tags, pools and an API for automation.

baremetal/hardware-failure-diagnosis-and.s: Hardware fails slowly and strangely. You read logs and sensors to find the failing part, prove it to the vendor and replace it without losing data.
baremetal/hardware-failure-diagnosis-and.i: I correlate the BMC system event log, kernel messages, SMART and ECC counters to isolate a part, drain the node, run vendor diagnostics, collect evidence for an RMA and verify after the swap. I track failure rates by model and batch.

baremetal/power-cooling-and-rack-capacit.s: A rack has a power budget and a heat budget. You add up what servers really draw, keep two feeds balanced and leave room so one failure does not take everything down.
baremetal/power-cooling-and-rack-capacit.i: I budget per-rack kilowatts using measured draw rather than nameplate, keep A and B feeds balanced so either can carry the load, watch inlet temperature and airflow, and track stranded capacity. I place hot equipment where cooling can support it.

baremetal/uefi-bootloaders-and-secure-bo.s: Before Linux starts, firmware picks a boot entry and loads a bootloader. Secure Boot checks that each piece is signed, which protects against tampered boot code.
baremetal/uefi-bootloaders-and-secure-bo.i: UEFI reads boot entries from NVRAM and loads a bootloader from the EFI system partition, which loads the kernel and initramfs. Secure Boot verifies signatures against enrolled keys. I manage entries with efibootmgr and plan for key and shim updates.

sql-ops/pg-stat-statements-and-query-tun.s: A database is often slow because of a handful of queries. pg_stat_statements counts every query shape so you can tune the ones that cost the most in total.
sql-ops/pg-stat-statements-and-query-tun.i: I enable pg_stat_statements, order by total_exec_time, mean time and calls, compare before and after with a reset, read plans for the top offenders and fix with indexes, rewrites or caching. Normalized queries hide values, so I log samples separately.

sql-ops/partitioning-and-data-retention.s: Huge tables get slow to maintain. Partitioning splits one table into smaller pieces so you can drop old data instantly and keep indexes small.
sql-ops/partitioning-and-data-retention.i: I use declarative range partitioning by time for logs and events, create partitions ahead of time, drop or detach old ones instead of deleting rows, keep the partition key in queries so the planner prunes, and automate creation with a scheduled job.

sql-ops/sql-backup-and-point-in-time-rec.s: A backup you have not restored is only a hope. You combine a base backup with the write-ahead log so you can return to the minute before a mistake.
sql-ops/sql-backup-and-point-in-time-rec.i: I take regular base backups, archive WAL continuously, store both off the server with retention, restore to a new host to a chosen timestamp and measure RPO and RTO. I run restore tests on a schedule and alert when archiving falls behind.

sql-ops/online-schema-changes-without-do.s: A simple ALTER TABLE can lock a busy table and stop an application. You make changes in small safe steps and set time limits so locks cannot pile up.
sql-ops/online-schema-changes-without-do.i: I set lock_timeout, add columns without volatile defaults, build indexes concurrently, backfill in small batches, add constraints as NOT VALID then validate, and use expand and contract across releases. I test the migration on realistic data size first.

sql-ops/replicas-failover-and-switchover.s: A replica keeps a copy of the data. You switch over on purpose for maintenance and fail over in emergencies, and you must make sure only one server accepts writes.
sql-ops/replicas-failover-and-switchover.i: I use streaming replication, watch replay lag in bytes and seconds, use a manager such as Patroni with a consensus store for automatic failover, fence the old primary to avoid split brain, rebuild old primaries as replicas and route clients through a stable endpoint.

sql-ops/autovacuum-bloat-and-maintenance.s: PostgreSQL leaves old row versions behind until vacuum cleans them. If vacuum falls behind, tables swell and queries slow, so you watch it and tune it.
sql-ops/autovacuum-bloat-and-maintenance.i: I monitor dead tuples, last autovacuum time and table size trends, tune scale factors and cost limits per hot table, find long transactions and replication slots that block cleanup, watch transaction ID age and use pg_repack or VACUUM FULL only in planned windows.

sql-ops/database-incident-runbook.s: When the database is struggling, follow a fixed order of checks. You confirm what users see, look for the usual causes and apply the smallest safe fix first.
sql-ops/database-incident-runbook.i: I triage with a runbook: confirm scope, check connections, long queries and locks, disk and I/O, replication and recent changes, mitigate with the least risky action such as killing a blocker, and capture evidence for the review. I avoid restarting as a first move.

service-mesh/sidecar-and-ambient-mesh-da.s: A mesh puts a proxy beside each app or on each node. Sidecars give strong per-pod control, while ambient mode shares proxies per node to save resources.
service-mesh/sidecar-and-ambient-mesh-da.i: Sidecar meshes inject an Envoy proxy into every pod, which costs memory and CPU and ties proxy upgrades to pod restarts. Ambient mode uses a per-node layer 4 proxy and optional layer 7 waypoint proxies. I choose by resource cost, feature needs and risk.

service-mesh/ingress-gateways-and-the-ga.s: A gateway is the front door of your cluster. It terminates TLS, routes requests to services and applies edge policy before traffic enters the mesh.
service-mesh/ingress-gateways-and-the-ga.i: The Kubernetes Gateway API separates infrastructure roles with GatewayClass, Gateway and HTTPRoute. I terminate TLS at the gateway, route by host and path, set timeouts and limits, and keep mesh-internal and edge policy distinct.

service-mesh/traffic-shifting-retries-an.s: A mesh can send 5 percent of traffic to a new version and retry failed calls. Used carelessly, retries multiply load and make outages worse.
service-mesh/traffic-shifting-retries-an.i: I use weighted routing for canaries, set per-try and overall timeouts, limit retries with budgets and idempotency, add circuit breaking and outlier detection, and watch error rate and latency per version while shifting weights.

service-mesh/mesh-authorization-and-zero.s: With mTLS every workload has an identity. Authorization policies use those identities to say who may call what, and deny everything else.
service-mesh/mesh-authorization-and-zero.i: I enforce strict mTLS, write AuthorizationPolicy with ALLOW rules by service account, namespace, method and path, start with a default deny per namespace, test in dry-run or audit first and review denials in logs before enforcing widely.

service-mesh/multi-cluster-mesh-and-fail.s: A multi-cluster mesh lets services in different clusters call each other and fail over between them. It needs shared trust and careful network design.
