service-mesh/multi-cluster-mesh-and-fail.i: Multi-cluster needs a shared root of trust, cross-cluster service discovery and reachable gateways or flat networking. I use locality-aware load balancing with failover, keep clusters independent enough to survive each other's failure, and test failover regularly.

service-mesh/mesh-performance-cost-and-r.s: A mesh adds work to every request. You measure the added latency and memory, trim what each proxy knows and tune telemetry so the cost stays reasonable.
service-mesh/mesh-performance-cost-and-r.i: I benchmark with and without the mesh, check proxy CPU, memory and added p99 latency, limit each workload's configuration with scoped sidecar resources, reduce high-cardinality metrics, size control plane resources and set proxy requests and limits.

service-mesh/operating-and-upgrading-a-s.s: A mesh is critical infrastructure, so upgrades need a plan. You run the new version beside the old, move workloads in stages and keep a way back.
service-mesh/operating-and-upgrading-a-s.i: I use revision-based canary upgrades, move namespaces with revision labels, restart workloads in waves, watch error rates and config push health, keep proxy and control plane versions within the supported skew and rehearse rollback.

gpu-serving/quantization-and-model-sizin.s: A model must fit in GPU memory before it can run. Quantization stores weights with fewer bits, so bigger models fit on smaller GPUs with a small loss in quality.
gpu-serving/quantization-and-model-sizin.i: Weight memory is parameters times bytes per parameter, plus KV cache and overhead. FP16 uses 2 bytes, INT8 uses 1 and 4-bit formats use about half a byte. I compare quality on my own evaluation set before choosing a format.

gpu-serving/batching-kv-cache-and-throug.s: A GPU is most efficient when it serves many requests at once. Continuous batching and a well-managed cache raise throughput without making every user wait.
gpu-serving/batching-kv-cache-and-throug.i: Prefill processes the prompt in parallel and decode generates tokens one by one. Continuous batching adds and removes requests every step, paged attention manages the KV cache without fragmentation, and limits such as max batch tokens and max sequences set the latency and throughput balance.

gpu-serving/multi-gpu-tensor-and-pipelin.s: When a model does not fit on one GPU, you split it across several. Fast links between GPUs matter a lot, so placement decides performance.
gpu-serving/multi-gpu-tensor-and-pipelin.i: Tensor parallelism splits each layer across GPUs and needs fast NVLink-class links. Pipeline parallelism assigns layers to stages and tolerates slower links. If a model fits one GPU, replicas usually give better throughput and simpler failure handling.

gpu-serving/autoscaling-llm-inference.s: CPU use is a poor signal for GPU model servers. You scale on queue depth or latency, keep some capacity warm because model loading is slow and cap spending.
gpu-serving/autoscaling-llm-inference.i: I scale on waiting requests, concurrency per replica or time to first token with KEDA or the HPA using custom metrics, set minimum replicas for warm capacity, use scale-down stabilization and cluster autoscaling for nodes, and set a maximum for cost control.

gpu-serving/model-loading-caching-and-co.s: Big model files take minutes to download and load. Caching them near the GPU and using fast formats makes restarts and scaling much quicker.
gpu-serving/model-loading-caching-and-co.i: I use safetensors, store weights on a fast shared or node-local volume, pre-pull container images, verify checksums, warm pools before routing traffic and use readiness probes that wait until the model is loaded and answers a test request.

gpu-serving/gpu-sharing-mig-and-time-sli.s: A whole GPU is too big for many small jobs. You can split it into isolated slices or let jobs take turns, each with different trade-offs.
gpu-serving/gpu-sharing-mig-and-time-sli.i: MIG creates hardware-isolated partitions with guaranteed memory and compute. Time-slicing shares a GPU by switching without memory isolation, and MPS lets processes run concurrently. I choose MIG for isolation and predictable latency, and time-slicing for light dev workloads.

gpu-serving/gpu-failures-xid-errors-and-.s: GPUs fail in specific ways and leave codes in the kernel log. You learn to read them, take the node out of service and decide between a reset and a replacement.
gpu-serving/gpu-failures-xid-errors-and-.i: I watch dmesg for Xid errors, use DCGM health checks and ECC counters, distinguish application faults from hardware faults, cordon and drain the node, try a reset when allowed and replace parts that repeat. I automate detection and node isolation.

aiops/telemetry-quality-for-aiops.s: AIOps tools are only as good as the data they read. Clean names, labels and time are worth more than a fancier model.
aiops/telemetry-quality-for-aiops.i: I standardize service names, labels and timestamps, fix clock skew, track missing data and cardinality, keep a service catalog as the join key between metrics, logs, traces and incidents, and measure data quality as a metric.

aiops/forecasting-capacity-and-saturatio.s: Instead of waiting for a disk to fill, you forecast when it will. Simple trend lines with weekly patterns catch most capacity problems early.
aiops/forecasting-capacity-and-saturatio.i: I use linear and seasonal forecasts on saturation metrics, alert on predicted time to full rather than current percentage, account for known events, review forecast error and keep models simple and explainable.

aiops/llm-assistants-for-incident-respon.s: A language model can summarize logs, draft status updates and find runbook steps quickly. It can also invent things, so a human checks anything that matters.
aiops/llm-assistants-for-incident-respon.i: I use LLMs for summarization, timeline drafts, runbook retrieval and stakeholder updates, ground answers in retrieved evidence with citations, redact sensitive data, require human approval for any action and log prompts and outputs for review.

aiops/measuring-aiops-value-and-avoiding.s: Does the tool actually help? You measure noise, detection time and resolution time before and after, and compare against a simple baseline.
aiops/measuring-aiops-value-and-avoiding.i: I define success metrics up front, such as alert volume, precision, recall, MTTD and MTTR, run a pilot with a control group or shadow mode, compare against a simple rule baseline, count the human cost of maintaining the tool and decide with data.

aiops/runbook-automation-and-guardrails.s: Automating a runbook saves time, but a script that acts on a wrong signal can make an outage worse. Guardrails keep automation safe.
aiops/runbook-automation-and-guardrails.i: I automate in stages: documented steps, a script a human runs, a script that suggests, then auto-run for low-risk actions. Each automation checks preconditions, supports dry run, limits blast radius with rate limits and circuit breakers, logs actions and has a rollback.

argocd/argocd-sso-rbac-and-audit.s: Argo CD can deploy to your clusters, so who may use it matters. You sign in with single sign-on, give roles the least they need and keep a record of actions.
argocd/argocd-sso-rbac-and-audit.i: I configure OIDC SSO, disable the local admin after bootstrapping, map groups to roles in argocd-rbac-cm, scope roles with AppProjects, restrict repositories and destinations, and send audit events and logs to central monitoring.

argocd/argocd-notifications-and-image-up.s: You want to hear when a deployment breaks, and you want new image versions to flow in without hand edits. Both can be done through Argo CD add-ons.
argocd/argocd-notifications-and-image-up.i: Argo CD Notifications sends messages on triggers such as sync failed or health degraded with templates and subscriptions. Image updating writes new tags to Git by policy, so deployments remain reviewable and reversible.

argocd/progressive-delivery-with-argo-ro.s: A normal Deployment replaces pods all at once. Argo Rollouts shifts traffic in steps and checks metrics, so a bad release is stopped before it reaches everyone.
argocd/progressive-delivery-with-argo-ro.i: A Rollout resource replaces a Deployment and defines canary steps with weights and pauses, or a blue-green switch. AnalysisTemplates query metrics such as error rate, and the rollout aborts and rolls back automatically on failure.

argocd/argocd-disaster-recovery-and-upgr.s: Argo CD itself must survive failures. Because Git holds the desired state, you can rebuild it quickly if you keep its own configuration and secrets safe.
argocd/argocd-disaster-recovery-and-upgr.i: I keep Argo CD configuration in Git, back up secrets and the Application and AppProject objects with argocd admin export, rehearse rebuilding a cluster from a bootstrap application, upgrade one minor version at a time after reading release notes and test in a non-production instance first.

claude-skills/skills-for-runbooks-and-op.s: A skill can hold a team's runbook so Claude follows the same steps every time. You write the order of checks, the safe commands and the points where a human must decide.
claude-skills/skills-for-runbooks-and-op.i: An operations skill states when it applies, lists ordered checks with exact commands, includes read-only scripts, marks stop points that need approval, and records what it found. I keep dangerous actions out of the skill or behind explicit confirmation.

claude-skills/skills-with-references-tem.s: A skill folder can hold more than one file. The main file stays short, and extra files hold details Claude reads only when needed.
claude-skills/skills-with-references-tem.i: SKILL.md holds the core instructions and links to reference files, templates and examples that load on demand. I keep each reference focused, name files clearly, avoid deep nesting and put rarely used detail outside the main file to save context.

claude-skills/organizing-skills-for-a-te.s: When many people write skills, you need rules. Clear names, owners and reviews keep skills useful and safe.
claude-skills/organizing-skills-for-a-te.i: I use consistent names and descriptions, give every skill an owner and a review cycle, keep skills in a repository with pull requests and tests, version changes, publish a catalog, and retire unused or risky skills.

claude-skills/evaluating-and-regression-.s: A skill is only as good as its results. You keep a set of test prompts with expected behavior and run them whenever the skill changes.
claude-skills/evaluating-and-regression-.i: I create positive and negative trigger tests, task tests with graded outputs, run them with and without the skill, check script behavior separately, record scores per version and require results not to regress before merging changes.

cloud-iam/gcp-iam-and-service-accounts.s: In Google Cloud you grant roles to identities on a resource, and permissions flow down the hierarchy. Service accounts are identities for workloads and should not use downloaded keys.
cloud-iam/gcp-iam-and-service-accounts.i: IAM binds principals to roles at organization, folder, project or resource level, with inheritance downward. I use predefined or custom roles, avoid basic roles, give workloads dedicated service accounts, use impersonation and workload identity instead of keys, and review with policy analysis.

cloud-iam/workload-identity-federation-a.s: Instead of storing a cloud key in your CI system, the cloud trusts a signed token that proves who the job is. Tokens are short-lived, and trust rules limit who may use them.
cloud-iam/workload-identity-federation-a.i: Federation uses OIDC: a workload gets a signed token from its platform, the cloud validates it against the issuer, and exchanges it for temporary credentials if claims such as repository, branch or service account match. I pin subject and audience in the trust policy.

cloud-iam/permission-boundaries-scps-and.s: Policies grant access, but guardrails set the maximum. An organization can say that no account may ever disable logging, whatever a local admin writes.
cloud-iam/permission-boundaries-scps-and.i: Service control policies limit what every identity in an account can do, permission boundaries cap what a role can be granted, and organization policies enforce settings. Effective permission is the intersection of grants and guardrails, and explicit deny wins.

cloud-iam/iam-policy-analysis-and-unused.s: Over time roles collect permissions nobody uses. Tools show what was actually used and who can reach what, so you can trim access with evidence.
cloud-iam/iam-policy-analysis-and-unused.i: I use access analyzers to find external and unused access, last-accessed data to shrink policies, policy simulators to test changes, generate least-privilege policies from logs and remove permissions in steps with monitoring for denials.

helm/testing-and-linting-helm-charts.s: A chart is code, so it needs tests. You lint it, render it, validate the output and try it on a throwaway cluster before anyone depends on it.
helm/testing-and-linting-helm-charts.i: I run helm lint and helm template in CI, validate rendered manifests with a Kubernetes schema checker, add a values.schema.json, write unit tests for templates and run chart-testing install and upgrade tests on a temporary cluster.

helm/library-charts-and-chart-reuse.s: Fifty services should not mean fifty copies of the same Deployment template. A library chart holds shared templates that each service chart reuses.
helm/library-charts-and-chart-reuse.i: A library chart has type library and provides named templates through include. Service charts depend on it and call its templates with their values. I version the library, keep its interface small and use umbrella charts only where services deploy together.

helm/publishing-and-signing-helm-charts.s: Charts are software artifacts. You package them, push them to a registry and sign them so users can verify where a chart came from.
helm/publishing-and-signing-helm-charts.i: I package charts with a version, push to an OCI registry, authenticate with short-lived tokens, sign with cosign or a provenance file and verify before install. Release from CI only and keep versions immutable.

helm/helm-security-and-supply-chain.s: A chart can create any Kubernetes object, including risky ones. You review what you install, scan what it renders and enforce policy at admission.
helm/helm-security-and-supply-chain.i: I pin chart and image versions, render and review third-party charts, scan manifests and images, avoid charts requesting privileged settings, limit who can install cluster-wide objects, keep secrets out of values files and enforce Pod Security and policy at admission.

k8s-ops/control-plane-monitoring-and-slo.s: The cluster's brain needs monitoring like any service. You watch the API server, etcd and controllers and set targets for how well the platform should work.
k8s-ops/control-plane-monitoring-and-slo.i: I scrape API server request latency and error rate, etcd commit and fsync latency and database size, scheduler and controller work queues and certificate expiry, alert on symptoms and define platform SLOs for API availability and scheduling latency.

k8s-ops/persistent-storage-and-csi-opera.s: Stateful apps need volumes that survive pods. You choose storage classes, expand volumes, snapshot them and fix volumes that will not attach or detach.
k8s-ops/persistent-storage-and-csi-opera.i: A StorageClass names a CSI provisioner and parameters. PVCs bind to PVs, volumes attach to nodes and mount into pods. I enable expansion, use snapshots and volume snapshot classes, set reclaim policy deliberately and debug attach and mount errors by reading events and CSI logs.

k8s-ops/multi-tenancy-namespaces-and-fai.s: Many teams can share one cluster if each gets a fenced area with limits. Namespaces, quotas and policies make the fences.
k8s-ops/multi-tenancy-namespaces-and-fai.i: I give each team namespaces with resource quotas, limit ranges, RBAC, network policies and policy controls, use priority classes and fair-share scheduling, label everything for cost and ownership, and use separate clusters when isolation needs are strict.

k8s-ops/cluster-disaster-recovery-runboo.s: If a cluster is lost, you should be able to rebuild it and restore the data. That takes a plan, backups and practice.
k8s-ops/cluster-disaster-recovery-runboo.i: I separate cluster rebuild, from infrastructure code and configuration in Git, from state recovery, with etcd and volume backups. I define RPO and RTO, back up secrets and certificates safely, rehearse a full rebuild and document the order of steps.

llm/embeddings-and-vector-search.s: An embedding turns text into a list of numbers so that similar meanings sit close together. Search then finds the nearest vectors instead of matching exact words.
llm/embeddings-and-vector-search.i: Embedding models map text to dense vectors, and cosine similarity or dot product measures closeness. I chunk documents sensibly, store vectors with metadata in an index such as HNSW, combine vector and keyword search and evaluate retrieval with real queries.

llm/retrieval-augmented-generation.s: A model does not know your documents. RAG searches them first and gives the best passages to the model, so answers come from your sources.
llm/retrieval-augmented-generation.i: RAG retrieves relevant chunks, builds a prompt with them and instructions to answer only from that context with citations, then returns the answer and sources. I evaluate retrieval and answer quality separately, handle no-result cases and enforce access controls at retrieval.

llm/fine-tuning-versus-prompting-versus-.s: When a model gives bad results, you can change the prompt, add retrieved documents or train it further. Each fixes a different kind of problem.
llm/fine-tuning-versus-prompting-versus-.i: Prompting fixes instructions and format, RAG supplies missing or changing knowledge and fine-tuning changes consistent style, format or narrow skills. I start with prompts and evaluation, add RAG for knowledge, and fine-tune only when a measured gap remains.

llm/llm-safety-privacy-and-data-handling.s: Prompts can contain private data and models can be tricked. You decide what leaves your systems, what is stored and how untrusted text is treated.
llm/llm-safety-privacy-and-data-handling.i: I classify data before sending it, redact secrets and personal data, choose providers and retention settings by policy, treat retrieved and user text as untrusted to resist prompt injection, limit tool permissions and log with care so logs do not become a leak.

mcp/designing-good-tools-for-agents.s: A model only knows what your tool descriptions tell it. Clear names, small inputs and useful error messages make the difference between a tool that works and one that confuses.
mcp/designing-good-tools-for-agents.i: I give tools specific names and descriptions of when to use them, keep inputs few and typed with enums, return concise structured results with identifiers, make errors actionable, separate read and write tools and add confirmation for destructive actions.

mcp/testing-and-debugging-mcp-servers-wi.s: Before connecting a server to a model, you test it directly. The MCP Inspector lets you call tools by hand and see the exact messages.
mcp/testing-and-debugging-mcp-servers-wi.i: I use the MCP Inspector to list and call tools, check schemas and outputs, write unit tests for tool functions and integration tests over stdio, log to stderr for stdio servers, validate inputs and compare behavior across clients.

mcp/deploying-and-scaling-mcp-servers.s: Local servers run on a developer's machine. Shared servers run remotely over HTTP, so they need authentication, limits and monitoring like any service.
mcp/deploying-and-scaling-mcp-servers.i: Remote MCP servers use streamable HTTP, authenticate clients with OAuth or tokens, run in containers with health checks and resource limits, apply rate limits and timeouts, keep state out of process where possible and emit logs, metrics and traces per tool call.

mcp/composing-multiple-mcp-servers.s: Real agents use tools from several servers at once. You keep each server focused, name tools clearly and limit how many tools the model must choose from.
mcp/composing-multiple-mcp-servers.i: A client can connect to many servers, and their tools appear together. I keep servers small and focused, namespace tools, limit which tools each agent sees, watch the context cost of many tool descriptions and test combinations for conflicting names and overlapping purposes.

mlops/feature-stores-and-data-versioning.s: A model fails quietly when training and serving compute features differently. A feature store defines each feature once, and dataset versions let you rebuild any model.
mlops/feature-stores-and-data-versioning.i: A feature store provides one definition for offline training data and online serving, with point-in-time correct joins to avoid leakage. I version datasets and feature definitions, record lineage from raw data to model and monitor feature freshness.

mlops/model-evaluation-ab-tests-and-shad.s: A better score on a test set does not prove a better product. You check slices of data, run the new model in shadow and then test it with a small share of real users.
mlops/model-evaluation-ab-tests-and-shad.i: I evaluate on held-out data with metrics tied to the goal, break results down by slice, run shadow deployments to compare outputs on live traffic without affecting users, then run A/B tests or canaries with guardrail metrics and a rollback plan.

mlops/ml-pipelines-and-workflow-orchestr.s: Training should be a pipeline anyone can rerun, not a notebook only one person understands. An orchestrator runs the steps, retries failures and records every run.
mlops/ml-pipelines-and-workflow-orchestr.i: I split work into steps such as ingest, validate, train, evaluate and register, run them on an orchestrator like Airflow, Argo Workflows or Kubeflow Pipelines, cache unchanged steps, pass artifacts by reference, set retries and resource requests, and trigger by schedule or data change.

mlops/llmops-prompts-evals-and-versionin.s: Prompts and model choices change behavior as much as code does. You version them, test them against examples and watch cost and quality in production.
mlops/llmops-prompts-evals-and-versionin.i: I store prompts in version control with variables and tests, pin model versions, run an evaluation suite on every change, release with canaries, track tokens, latency and cost per request, log traces and collect feedback to grow the test set.

openstack/cinder-glance-and-storage-serv.s: Cinder provides block volumes for instances, and Glance stores the images they boot from. Both usually sit on shared storage such as Ceph.
openstack/cinder-glance-and-storage-serv.i: Cinder creates and attaches volumes through backend drivers, supports snapshots and backups and enforces quotas. Glance stores images with properties. With Ceph, volumes and images are RBD objects, so boot from volume and copy-on-write clones are fast.

openstack/horizon-heat-and-openstack-aut.s: Clicking in a dashboard does not scale. You automate with the CLI, SDKs and templates, so environments are repeatable.
openstack/horizon-heat-and-openstack-aut.i: Horizon is the web dashboard, the openstack CLI and SDKs call the same APIs, Heat describes stacks in templates, and Terraform's OpenStack provider is an alternative. I keep infrastructure in code, use application credentials and clean up with stack deletion.

openstack/deploying-openstack-with-kolla.s: Kolla-Ansible installs OpenStack services as containers on your hosts using Ansible. You describe the cluster in a few files and it does the rest.
openstack/deploying-openstack-with-kolla.i: Kolla builds service containers and Kolla-Ansible deploys them from an inventory with globals.yml and passwords.yml. I use bootstrap, prechecks, deploy and post-deploy steps, override configuration per service, use rolling upgrades and keep configuration in version control.

openstack/openstack-monitoring-and-capac.s: A cloud needs two views: is the control plane healthy and is there room for new workloads. You collect metrics for both and plan before you run out.
openstack/openstack-monitoring-and-capac.i: I monitor API latency and errors per service, RabbitMQ queues, the database, Ceph health, nova-compute heartbeats and hypervisor usage, track overcommit and free capacity per flavor, forecast growth and set quotas that reflect real capacity.

prompting/prompting-for-code-and-infrast.s: Models write useful scripts and configs when you give them the context, limits and a way to check the result. You still run tests and review before anything reaches production.
prompting/prompting-for-code-and-infrast.i: I supply the environment, versions, constraints and expected behavior, ask for small diffs with explanations, request tests and edge cases, run linters and dry runs, and never apply generated infrastructure changes without a plan or review.

prompting/prompt-injection-and-defensive.s: Text a model reads can contain instructions. If your application lets the model act, a hidden instruction in an email or web page may try to take control.
prompting/prompt-injection-and-defensive.i: Direct injection comes from the user, indirect injection hides in content the model reads. I separate instructions from data, minimize tool permissions, require approval for sensitive actions, validate outputs and tool arguments, restrict data flows and test with adversarial examples.

prompting/agents-and-multi-step-workflow.s: A workflow follows steps you define. An agent decides its own steps in a loop. Agents are flexible, and workflows are predictable. Many tasks only need a workflow.
prompting/agents-and-multi-step-workflow.i: I prefer fixed workflows such as chaining, routing and parallel steps when the path is known, and use an agent loop with tools when the path is not known. I set step and cost limits, checkpoints, logging, error handling and human approval for risky actions.

prompting/evaluating-prompts-with-datase.s: You cannot improve a prompt you cannot measure. A small set of real examples with expected answers tells you whether a change helped.
prompting/evaluating-prompts-with-datase.i: I collect real inputs, label expected outputs or criteria, define exact and rubric checks, run each prompt version over the set, compare scores and cost, spot-check model graders against human labels and grow the set from production failures.

virtualization/vm-backup-replication-and.s: A VM is a file plus configuration, so it can be copied. But a good backup must be consistent and restorable, and you only know that by testing it.
virtualization/vm-backup-replication-and.i: I use application-consistent snapshots with guest agents, back up changed blocks, keep copies off the primary storage, replicate to a second site for fast failover, set retention by policy and test restores including network and boot checks.

virtualization/vm-templates-cloud-init-a.s: Hand-made templates drift and nobody knows what is in them. An image pipeline builds a fresh, tested image from code every time.
virtualization/vm-templates-cloud-init-a.i: I build images with Packer or similar from a base ISO or cloud image, apply configuration with Ansible, harden and scan the result, remove machine-specific data, test boot with cloud-init and publish versioned images. Instances get identity from cloud-init, not from the image.

virtualization/gpu-passthrough-and-devic.s: Passthrough hands a physical device, such as a GPU, directly to one VM. The VM gets near-native speed, but the host and other VMs lose access to it.
virtualization/gpu-passthrough-and-devic.i: PCI passthrough uses the IOMMU and the VFIO driver to assign a device to a guest. I enable IOMMU, check IOMMU groups, bind the device to vfio-pci, attach it to the VM and plan for no live migration and for host reset behavior.

virtualization/hypervisor-security-and-i.s: A hypervisor holds many machines, so a mistake there reaches all of them. You keep it patched, limit who manages it and separate what guests can see.
virtualization/hypervisor-security-and-i.i: I minimize the hypervisor attack surface, patch quickly, restrict and log management access, isolate management, storage and guest networks, use sVirt or equivalent confinement, protect images and snapshots, apply CPU mitigations as advised and separate workloads by trust.

ansible/ansible-performance-and-executio.s: Ansible gets slow on big fleets if you leave the defaults. A few settings make runs much faster and safer.
ansible/ansible-performance-and-executio.i: I raise forks, enable SSH pipelining and ControlPersist, cache or disable fact gathering, use async for long tasks, choose strategies such as free, and roll out with serial batches, max_fail_percentage and run_once for single-host steps.

ansible/writing-custom-ansible-modules-a.s: When no module does what you need, you can write one in Python. It must report changes honestly and be safe to run again.
ansible/writing-custom-ansible-modules-a.i: A custom module reads arguments, checks the current state, changes only when needed, supports check mode and returns changed and facts as JSON. Filters transform data in templates. I test them with unit tests and use existing modules first.

git/git-internals-objects-refs-and-the-i.s: Git stores snapshots as objects named by their hash. Branches are just small files pointing at commits, which is why they are cheap.
git/git-internals-objects-refs-and-the-i.i: Git has four object types: blob, tree, commit and tag, addressed by content hash. Refs such as branches and tags point to commits, HEAD points to a ref, and the index is the staging area for the next tree. I use plumbing commands to inspect and recover state.

git/release-and-hotfix-workflows-with-gi.s: Releases need a stable point in history and a way to fix bugs in it without taking everything new. Branches, tags and cherry-pick give you that.
git/release-and-hotfix-workflows-with-gi.i: I tag releases with annotated, signed tags, create release branches when several versions need support, develop hotfixes from the release tag or branch, cherry-pick fixes to other branches with the -x flag and automate versioning and changelogs from commit messages.

go/configuration-logging-and-metrics-in-.s: A service needs settings from outside, logs people can search and metrics for dashboards. Go's standard library and one small client cover all three.
go/configuration-logging-and-metrics-in-.i: I load configuration with flags and environment variables with validation and defaults, log structured JSON with log/slog and request IDs, expose a metrics endpoint with the Prometheus client, add health endpoints and keep secrets out of logs.

go/writing-kubernetes-clients-and-contro.s: Operators and controllers are Go programs that watch Kubernetes and make the world match a desired state. Informers and queues make that efficient and reliable.
go/writing-kubernetes-clients-and-contro.i: client-go talks to the API server. Informers cache objects and deliver events, work queues deduplicate and retry keys, and a reconcile function compares desired and actual state and acts idempotently. I use controller-runtime for real controllers and add leader election and metrics.

bash/log-analysis-one-liners-and-pipelin.s: Most incidents start with a log file and a question. A few commands piped together can count errors, find slow requests and show who is calling most.
bash/log-analysis-one-liners-and-pipelin.i: I filter with grep or awk, extract fields with cut and awk, aggregate with sort and uniq -c, compute percentiles with sort and awk, parse JSON logs with jq, work in streaming fashion with tail -F and keep useful pipelines in a script.

databases/database-observability-and-cap.s: Database problems build slowly and then hit suddenly. The right handful of metrics show trouble early and let you plan growth.
databases/database-observability-and-cap.i: I track the golden signals per database: latency, traffic, errors and saturation, plus connections, locks, replication lag, cache hit ratio, disk and WAL growth. I alert on symptoms and time to full, and forecast capacity from trends.

storage/storage-benchmarking-with-fio.s: A single speed number does not describe storage. fio lets you test the access pattern your application actually uses and read the latency, not just the throughput.
storage/storage-benchmarking-with-fio.i: I use fio with direct I/O and job files that match the workload: block size, random or sequential, read-write mix, queue depth and number of jobs, then read IOPS, bandwidth and latency percentiles. I test on a scratch volume and compare with the provider's limits.

security/web-and-api-attacks-for-operato.s: Most web attacks abuse a few ideas: trusting input, skipping an access check or letting the server make requests for the attacker. Operators see them first in logs.
security/web-and-api-attacks-for-operato.i: Injection, broken access control, SSRF, insecure deserialization and API abuse are common causes of breaches. I recognize patterns in logs, use parameterized queries, enforce authorization on the server, restrict outbound requests, apply rate limits and a web application firewall and test regularly.

security/sast-dast-and-dependency-scanni.s: Scanners find problems early, but too many findings train people to ignore them. You choose the right tools, tune them and block only on what matters.
security/sast-dast-and-dependency-scanni.i: SAST analyzes source, SCA scans dependencies, DAST tests a running app, and secret and IaC scanners check other risks. I run fast scans on every pull request, deeper ones on a schedule, set severity thresholds, triage with owners and SLAs and track false positives.

security/cloud-posture-and-misconfigurat.s: Most cloud breaches come from settings, not clever exploits. Posture management checks your accounts continuously for risky configuration and drift.
security/cloud-posture-and-misconfigurat.i: I scan with a cloud security posture tool and IaC scanners, use benchmarks such as CIS, prioritize by exposure and data sensitivity, fix findings in the infrastructure code instead of by hand, add guardrails to prevent recurrence and track time to remediate.

security/security-champions-and-secure-c.s: Security cannot be a gate at the end. Champions inside teams and short review checklists catch issues where they are cheapest to fix.
security/security-champions-and-secure-c.i: I run a champions program with training, time and a direct line to the security team, use small checklists for review of authentication, authorization, input handling, secrets and logging, threat model new features briefly and track recurring issues to improve libraries and templates.

security/incident-forensics-and-evidence.s: In a breach, what you do first can destroy evidence. You preserve what matters, record each step and build a timeline before cleaning up.
security/incident-forensics-and-evidence.i: I contain without destroying evidence, capture volatile data first, snapshot disks and export cloud logs to protected storage, hash and document everything for chain of custody, build a timeline from multiple sources and involve legal and management early.

security/audit-readiness-and-continuous-.s: Audits ask you to prove that your controls work. If evidence is collected automatically all year, an audit is a review, not a scramble.
security/audit-readiness-and-continuous-.i: I map each control to a technical check and an owner, collect evidence automatically from systems such as access reviews, change records and scan results, keep an immutable log, track exceptions and run internal reviews before the external audit.

cicd/jenkins-architecture-controllers-ag.s: Jenkins is a server that waits for a trigger, picks a worker machine called an agent, and runs the steps you defined. The controller is the brain; agents do the work.
cicd/jenkins-architecture-controllers-ag.i: The controller holds configuration, the queue, build history and credentials, and schedules builds onto agents by label. Jobs define what to run; builds are individual runs. Everything lives in JENKINS_HOME, so backups and disk space matter.

cicd/jenkins-declarative-pipelines-and-t.s: A Jenkinsfile is a text file in your repository that tells Jenkins what to build. It lists stages, and each stage lists steps.
cicd/jenkins-declarative-pipelines-and-t.i: Declarative syntax gives a fixed structure: pipeline, agent, environment, stages, post. Use when conditions, parallel stages and options such as timeout and retry to control flow, and keep the real work in scripts.

cicd/jenkins-build-agents-with-docker-an.s: Instead of keeping build machines forever, start a fresh container for each build and throw it away after.
cicd/jenkins-build-agents-with-docker-an.i: Static agents drift and accumulate state. Docker agents give a clean image per build, and the Kubernetes plugin starts an agent pod per build from a pod template, so capacity follows demand and tools are versioned in images.

cicd/jenkins-shared-libraries-and-reusab.s: A shared library is a repository of pipeline code that many projects can call, so you fix a mistake once instead of in fifty Jenkinsfiles.
cicd/jenkins-shared-libraries-and-reusab.i: Libraries load from a Git repository by version, expose steps in a vars/ directory and helpers in src/. Pin versions, test with a sandbox job and keep each step small and documented.

cicd/jenkins-credentials-security-and-ha.s: Jenkins holds the keys to your servers, so lock it down: store secrets properly, give people only the access they need and update it often.
cicd/jenkins-credentials-security-and-ha.i: Use the credentials store with scoped IDs and masking, role-based authorization, an SSO login, no builds on the controller, script approval for sandboxed code and prompt patching of the core and plugins.

cicd/jenkins-plugins-upgrades-and-operat.s: Jenkins grows by plugins and by agents. Keep both under control: pin versions, upgrade on a schedule and write down the setup as code.
cicd/jenkins-plugins-upgrades-and-operat.i: Describe the controller with Jenkins Configuration as Code, list plugins in a file, upgrade the LTS line in a test instance first, monitor queue time and executor use, and keep backups restorable.

cicd/jenkins-debugging-and-migrating-to-.s: When a Jenkins build is stuck or slow, check the queue, then the agent, then the log. If you decide to move to another tool, move one pipeline at a time.
cicd/jenkins-debugging-and-migrating-to-.i: Use the queue reason, node status, thread dump and replay to debug. For a migration, inventory jobs, move build logic into scripts, translate triggers and credentials, run both systems in parallel and retire old jobs on a schedule.

linux/debugging-with-strace-system-calls.s: strace shows every request a program makes to the operating system. When a program fails with a vague message, the last failing request usually tells you why.
linux/debugging-with-strace-system-calls.i: strace -f -tt -e trace=... follows children and times calls. Look for ENOENT, EACCES and ECONNREFUSED, blocked calls such as futex or poll, and the file or address involved. Use -c for a summary and attach with -p. It slows the target, so use it briefly.

linux/seeing-the-network-with-ss-and-tcp.s: ss shows which programs are listening and connected. tcpdump shows the actual packets on the wire. Together they tell you where a connection breaks.
linux/seeing-the-network-with-ss-and-tcp.i: Use ss -ltnp for listeners and ss -tn state for connections, then tcpdump -ni IFACE with a host, port and flags filter. SYN with no SYN-ACK means blocked or dropped; RST means refused; retransmissions mean loss.

linux/open-files-and-proc-with-lsof.s: Every open file and socket is a numbered handle. lsof lists them, and /proc shows them for any process, so you can find who is holding a disk, a port or a lock.
linux/open-files-and-proc-with-lsof.i: lsof -p PID, lsof -i :PORT and lsof +L1 answer who has it open. /proc/PID/fd, limits, status and cmdline show handles, limits and memory. A growing fd count is a leak; a deleted file still open keeps disk space.

linux/finding-cpu-memory-and-io-hogs.s: A slow server is short of CPU, memory or disk. A few commands show which one it is and which process is using it.
linux/finding-cpu-memory-and-io-hogs.i: Read load average against core count, then top for CPU and memory, vmstat for run queue, swap and I/O wait, iostat -x for disk utilisation and await, and pidstat for per-process numbers. High wa or swap in/out means the bottleneck is not the CPU.

linux/kernel-messages-journal-and-core-d.s: When something crashes the evidence is in the kernel log, the journal and sometimes a core file. Learn where each one is and how to read it.
linux/kernel-messages-journal-and-core-d.i: dmesg -T shows kernel events such as OOM kills and disk errors. journalctl -u, -p, -b and --since filter the journal. coredumpctl lists crashes and opens them in gdb. Persisting the journal across reboots keeps the evidence of the last crash.

linux/ebpf-and-bpftrace-live-questions.s: eBPF lets you run small, safe programs inside the Linux kernel to count and time events without changing the app. bpftrace turns a one-line question into such a program.
linux/ebpf-and-bpftrace-live-questions.i: eBPF programs attach to probes (tracepoints, kprobes, uprobes), are verified by the kernel before they run and report through maps. bpftrace gives a short language for them, and tools like execsnoop, opensnoop and biolatency are ready-made. Overhead is low but not zero.

linux/debugging-a-slow-or-hung-server-a-.s: Debugging a slow server is easier with a fixed order of questions. Ask what is slow, what is short, who is using it and what changed.
linux/debugging-a-slow-or-hung-server-a-.i: Use a USE-style walk through CPU, memory, disk and network (utilisation, saturation, errors), narrow to a process, then to a call or a log line, form one hypothesis, change one thing and measure again. Write down what you saw so the next person starts ahead.

proxies/what-a-reverse-proxy-does.s: A reverse proxy is a server that receives requests on behalf of your apps and passes them on. Users talk to the proxy, never to the app directly.
proxies/what-a-reverse-proxy-does.i: A reverse proxy terminates connections, routes by host and path, adds headers, can end TLS, balance, cache and limit traffic, and hides the backends. A forward proxy serves clients going out; a load balancer is a proxy focused on spreading load.

proxies/nginx-configuration-servers-and-.s: nginx reads a text file made of nested blocks. A server block matches a site, and location blocks match the path of a request.
proxies/nginx-configuration-servers-and-.i: Directives live in contexts (main, events, http, server, location). server_name and listen choose the server; location uses exact, prefix, regex and ^~ matching with a fixed order. nginx -t checks syntax and nginx -s reload applies it without dropping connections.

proxies/proxying-to-upstreams-headers-an.s: When nginx passes a request to an app it should also tell the app who the user is and which host was asked for. It must also handle long-lived connections like WebSockets.
proxies/proxying-to-upstreams-headers-an.i: proxy_pass sends requests to an upstream; proxy_set_header passes Host, X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto; proxy_http_version 1.1 with Upgrade headers supports WebSockets; buffering helps normal responses but hurts streaming. A trailing slash in proxy_pass changes the path sent.

proxies/tls-termination-http2-and-certif.s: The proxy holds the certificate and does the encryption with users. Keep the settings modern and renew certificates automatically.
proxies/tls-termination-http2-and-certif.i: Configure listen 443 ssl with http2, a full-chain certificate, TLS 1.2 and 1.3, session reuse, HSTS and a redirect from port 80. Automate renewal with ACME clients and watch expiry. Choose re-encryption to backends when the internal network is not trusted.

proxies/load-balancing-algorithms-and-he.s: A load balancer shares requests among several servers and stops sending to the ones that fail.
proxies/load-balancing-algorithms-and-he.i: Round robin, weighted, least connections and hash methods suit different loads; ip_hash or a hash on a key gives stickiness. Passive checks mark a server down after failures; active checks probe a health endpoint. Slow start and connection draining protect servers during changes.

proxies/timeouts-retries-keepalive-and-l.s: A proxy has several timers. If they are wrong, healthy requests are cut off or slow ones hold connections forever.
proxies/timeouts-retries-keepalive-and-l.i: connect, send and read timeouts apply to the backend leg; client timeouts to the user leg. keepalive reuses connections to the backend; worker_connections and file limits cap concurrency. Retries amplify load, so cap them and keep timeouts shorter than the caller above.

proxies/caching-compression-and-static-f.s: A proxy can answer repeat requests from memory or disk so the backend does less work. Compression makes responses smaller.
proxies/caching-compression-and-static-f.i: sendfile and open_file_cache speed static files; proxy_cache with a key, valid times, stale serving and locking protect backends; gzip or brotli compress text. Never cache personalised responses without varying the key, and purge or version assets deliberately.

proxies/rate-limiting-and-protecting-bac.s: A rate limit says how many requests one client may make. It keeps one noisy client from slowing everyone.
proxies/rate-limiting-and-protecting-bac.i: limit_req uses a leaky bucket with burst and nodelay; limit_conn caps concurrent connections; the key (address, token, API key) decides who is counted. Return 429 with Retry-After, whitelist health checks, and combine with timeouts and body limits. Behind a CDN, key on the real client address.

proxies/haproxy-frontends-backends-and-a.s: HAProxy is a fast load balancer. A frontend listens, a backend holds servers, and ACLs decide which backend gets a request.
proxies/haproxy-frontends-backends-and-a.i: Sections global, defaults, frontend, backend; ACLs match host, path, headers or source; use_backend and default_backend route; check, inter, rise and fall control health; stick tables track clients; the runtime socket and stats page expose live state and allow drain without reload.

proxies/envoy-traefik-and-dynamic-proxie.s: Some proxies change their routes without a reload when services come and go. Envoy, Traefik and Caddy all work this way, in different styles.
proxies/envoy-traefik-and-dynamic-proxie.i: Envoy uses listeners, routes, clusters and endpoints, updated over xDS; Traefik reads labels or Kubernetes resources through providers with entrypoints, routers and services; Caddy gives automatic HTTPS with a short Caddyfile. Choose by environment, observability needs and who writes configuration.

proxies/zero-downtime-reloads-and-blue-g.s: A proxy can reload without cutting users off, and it can send a small share of traffic to a new version first. Both reduce the risk of a change.
proxies/zero-downtime-reloads-and-blue-g.i: Graceful reload keeps old workers until requests finish. Blue-green switches an upstream atomically; canary uses weights or headers to send a small share first. Drain, readiness checks, and a tested rollback complete the routine.

proxies/debugging-502-504-and-proxy-prob.s: When users see 502 or 504 the proxy is the messenger. Check the proxy log, then the backend, to see which side failed.
proxies/debugging-502-504-and-proxy-prob.i: 502 means a bad or no response from the upstream; 503 means no available upstream or deliberate overload; 504 means timeout. Compare proxy timings with direct backend requests, read error.log for the reason, log $upstream_status and $upstream_response_time, and check DNS caching of upstream names.

messaging/queues-logs-and-pub-sub-choosi.s: Systems send messages so that the sender does not have to wait for the receiver. A queue hands each message to one worker; a log keeps messages so many readers can replay them.
messaging/queues-logs-and-pub-sub-choosi.i: A queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) delivers each message to one consumer and removes it. Pub/sub fans a message out to many subscribers. A log (Kafka) appends messages in order and keeps them for a time so consumers track their own position and can replay.

messaging/delivery-guarantees-ordering-a.s: Networks lose and repeat messages. Most systems choose to repeat rather than lose, so consumers must cope with the same message arriving twice.
messaging/delivery-guarantees-ordering-a.i: At-most-once may lose messages; at-least-once may duplicate; exactly-once end to end needs idempotent processing or transactions. Ordering usually holds only within one partition or queue. Use idempotency keys, deduplication tables and upserts, and order by a key.

messaging/rabbitmq-exchanges-queues-and-.s: In RabbitMQ producers send to an exchange, not to a queue. The exchange looks at routing rules called bindings and places copies in the right queues.
messaging/rabbitmq-exchanges-queues-and-.i: Exchange types direct, topic, fanout and headers route by routing key or headers to bound queues; durable queues and persistent messages survive restarts; vhosts separate environments; the management UI and rabbitmqctl show queues, consumers and message rates.

messaging/rabbitmq-acknowledgements-pref.s: A consumer tells the broker when it has finished with a message. If it crashes first the message goes back to the queue. Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue.
messaging/rabbitmq-acknowledgements-pref.i: Manual acks give at-least-once. Prefetch limits unacknowledged messages per consumer to spread load and bound memory. Reject with requeue false, or time-limit messages, to route to a dead-letter exchange; use delayed retry queues with TTL; monitor ready, unacked and consumer counts.

messaging/kafka-topics-partitions-and-br.s: Kafka stores messages in topics. A topic is split into partitions, each an ordered log on disk. More partitions mean more parallel readers.
messaging/kafka-topics-partitions-and-br.i: Records are appended to a partition chosen by key or round robin; each has an offset. Brokers host partitions; replicas copy them; a controller coordinates (KRaft mode replaces ZooKeeper). Ordering holds per partition; partition count sets maximum consumer parallelism and is hard to reduce.

messaging/kafka-producers-consumers-and-.s: Producers choose how sure they want to be that a record was saved. Consumers in a group split the partitions and commit their position as they go.
messaging/kafka-producers-consumers-and-.i: Producer settings acks, retries, idempotence, batching and compression; consumers poll, process, then commit offsets; groups assign partitions via a coordinator and rebalance when members change; commit after processing for at-least-once; static membership and cooperative rebalancing reduce disruption.

messaging/kafka-replication-isr-and-dura.s: Every partition has copies on other brokers. If the leader dies, a follower takes over. Settings decide how many copies must have a record before it counts as saved.
messaging/kafka-replication-isr-and-dura.i: Replication factor sets copies; ISR is the caught-up set; acks=all plus min.insync.replicas defines durability and availability; unclean leader election trades data for uptime; rack awareness spreads replicas; controlled shutdown moves leaders before a restart.

messaging/kafka-retention-compaction-and.s: Kafka deletes old data by age or size, or keeps only the latest record for each key. That choice decides how much disk you need and what consumers can replay.
messaging/kafka-retention-compaction-and.i: retention.ms and retention.bytes delete whole segments; cleanup.policy=compact keeps the latest value per key and uses tombstones to delete; segment size and index settings affect cleanup timing; disks need headroom, and tiered storage moves old segments to object storage.

messaging/kafka-lag-rebalances-and-capac.s: Operating Kafka means watching how far consumers are behind, whether replicas are healthy and whether disks and networks have room.
messaging/kafka-lag-rebalances-and-capac.i: Track consumer lag and its trend, under-replicated and offline partitions, request latency, ISR shrink events, disk, network and controller state. Respond to lag by checking consumer health before adding partitions; plan capacity with headroom and rolling restarts.

messaging/managed-messaging-on-cloud-sqs.s: Cloud providers run queues and streams for you. You trade some control for much less operating work.
messaging/managed-messaging-on-cloud-sqs.i: SQS is a queue and SNS a topic; Pub/Sub combines topics and subscriptions; Service Bus offers queues and topics with sessions; Event Hubs and Kinesis are partitioned logs; MSK and Confluent run Kafka for you. Check limits, ordering, retention, cost per request and portability.

messaging/schemas-contracts-and-evolving.s: A message is a contract between teams. When the format changes, old readers and old data must still work, so change it in compatible steps.
messaging/schemas-contracts-and-evolving.i: Schemas describe fields and types; Avro and Protobuf are compact and carry evolution rules; a schema registry stores versions and enforces compatibility modes (backward, forward, full). Add optional fields with defaults, never reuse or retype a field, and expand then contract for breaking changes.

messaging/debugging-messaging-incidents.s: Messaging problems show up as a growing backlog, missing messages, duplicates or wrong order. Each has a short list of causes to check in order.
messaging/debugging-messaging-incidents.i: For backlog: consumer alive, processing slow, producer burst, partition skew. For loss: acks, retention, routing, unclean elections. For duplicates: redelivery, retries, rebalances. For order: partitions, retries, multiple consumers. Trace one message by id from producer to consumer, and keep dead letters visible.

cfn-bicep/native-iac-cloudformation-bice.s: Each big cloud ships its own infrastructure-as-code language. They are tightly integrated with the platform and free to use, but only work on one cloud.
cfn-bicep/native-iac-cloudformation-bice.i: CloudFormation uses YAML or JSON templates and stacks; Bicep compiles to ARM templates and deploys through Azure Resource Manager. Both keep state in the cloud service, support new features early and need no state file. Terraform works across clouds but needs state storage.

cfn-bicep/cloudformation-templates-param.s: A template lists resources with their properties. Parameters make it reusable, outputs hand values to other stacks, and the stack is the running copy.
cfn-bicep/cloudformation-templates-param.i: Sections Parameters, Resources, Outputs, Conditions, Mappings; resource Type and Properties; Ref and Fn::GetAtt; aws cloudformation deploy and validate-template; logical id versus physical name; avoid hard-coded names to allow replacement.

cfn-bicep/intrinsic-functions-conditions.s: Intrinsic functions compute values at deployment time. Conditions switch resources on and off, and mappings are lookup tables.
cfn-bicep/intrinsic-functions-conditions.i: Fn::Ref, GetAtt, Sub, Join, Select, Split, ImportValue, If, Equals, FindInMap; Conditions create resources only when true; Mappings map region or environment to values; pseudo parameters like AWS::Region; SSM parameter types for latest AMIs.

cfn-bicep/stacks-change-sets-and-safe-up.s: Updating a stack can change a resource in place or replace it with a new one. A change set shows which before anything happens.
cfn-bicep/stacks-change-sets-and-safe-up.i: Create a change set, read Action and Replacement, execute or delete it; update behaviours No interruption, Some interruption, Replacement; UpdateReplacePolicy and DeletionPolicy; stack policies and termination protection; rollback on failure.

cfn-bicep/nested-stacks-stacksets-and-re.s: Big templates become hard to change. Nested stacks split them, and StackSets deploy one template to many accounts and regions.
cfn-bicep/nested-stacks-stacksets-and-re.i: Nested stacks use AWS::CloudFormation::Stack with TemplateURL; limits of 500 resources per stack; exports and ImportValue couple stacks; StackSets with service-managed permissions in Organizations; CloudFormation modules and registry; cross-stack references via SSM parameters.

cfn-bicep/drift-rollbacks-and-resource-p.s: People change resources in the console. Drift detection finds where reality no longer matches the template, and import brings unmanaged resources under control.
cfn-bicep/drift-rollbacks-and-resource-p.i: detect-stack-drift and describe-stack-resource-drifts; import existing resources into a stack; DeletionPolicy Retain; ROLLBACK_COMPLETE needs deleting before retry; UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED continue-update-rollback; stack policies, IAM guardrails and CloudTrail to find who changed what.

cfn-bicep/bicep-syntax-resources-and-par.s: Bicep is a short, typed language for Azure. You declare resources and let Azure Resource Manager work out the order.
